title: The key never reaches the store: detect, mask, and record the fact
description: Go+contracts only; the frontend chip and picker are a later round. internal/secrets ported from hermes redact.py (MIT, Nous Research): prefix table with boundary guard, structural rules (env assignment, auth header, JWT, private key, db connstring, url userinfo), entropy only in a value position at len>=32. Mask head=4 tail=4 floor=12. Masking happens at ws_history_record.go, the single writer of durable rows. The fact is recorded: count+kinds on the row, on history.record's result and on history.query's entries, so a block says '3 secrets masked' instead of masking silently. Contracts + over-the-wire tests. No migration for the content.db schema change (greenfield).
acceptance_criteria: Record a curl carrying a real key shape over the real socket, restart the composition root, query it back: the row reads sk-p...7890, the entry says one secret was masked and of what kind, and the raw key appears nowhere in the marshalled result (grep the whole payload). A commit SHA, a UUID and a long path in a command are left untouched.
close_reason: internal/secrets + masking at ws_history_record.go; count/kinds on the row and both contracts; app-level acceptance across restart; five review defects fixed (isReference guard, bare-token URL rule dropped, dead validator removed)

title: The first Tab skips the suggestion the user is looking at
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

Owner, 2026-08-02, four reports with screenshots:

1. Type `cd ` — the ghost suggestion is too bright and reads as typed text.
2. The ghost shows `Downloads/`; press Tab to take it and the selection jumps to the NEXT
   directory instead.
3. Every Tab press makes the dropdown narrower.
4. A whole-line history row (`rm zzz-e2e-cmp-msbojbc7`, naming a file since deleted) sits
   at the bottom of a list of path candidates and looks out of place.

## Root cause

Report 2 is an interaction-model error in the brief that produced the previous pass, not in
the code that implemented it. The rule given was "the first Tab opens, each further Tab
moves" — which ignores that the GHOST appears while typing, before any Tab. So the user is
already looking at candidate #1 when they press Tab for the first time, and being moved to #2
skips what is on screen.

Report 3: the panel re-measured its content on every render, so a narrower selected row
shrank it.

Report 4 is a category error the UI never expressed: a path candidate replaces the current
TOKEN, a history candidate replaces the WHOLE LINE. Two different actions, distinguished only
by a grey word on the right.

## Fixed by

Tab's rule, now written as a three-line table at the branch: ghost showing and dropdown closed
→ the first Tab opens with THAT candidate selected and does not advance; dropdown open → Tab
moves, Shift+Tab back; accept stays Enter (and Right/End for the ghost). The selection is
seeded by candidate id, so a history-first batch cannot steal it.

The ghost is the theme's text colour at 50% alpha (color-mix on the token, no literal). Width
is measured once per list content. History rows get their own captioned group at the end, and
a history candidate whose trailing token is a path that no longer exists is ranked last rather
than hidden — re-running a command to watch it fail is legitimate, and hiding history because
the filesystem moved would misreport what was run. The existence check reuses fs.complete, one
cached call per token, and is skipped entirely on a remote session where we cannot know.

## Acceptance Criteria

Type `cd ` in a directory with several subdirectories: the ghost shows the first candidate,
the first Tab settles on it rather than advancing, the second moves to the next, and the
panel's width does not change between presses.
close_reason: Shipped in e081df2. Verified by the coordinator in a real browser (three subdirectories): the ghost reads alpha/ before any Tab, the first Tab settles there rather than advancing, the second and third move to beta/ and gamma/, the panel stays 458px across all three, and the ghost renders at 50% alpha against fully opaque typed text. NOT verified by the coordinator: the history group caption and the stale-path demotion — the fixture had no history entries carrying paths; the worker's own tests and e2e cover them.

title: Completion says nothing when it has nothing, and the panel is a banner
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

Owner, 2026-08-02, four reports with screenshots:

1. The dropdown spans the whole pane width.
2. After `cd Downloads/`, Tab does nothing.
3. After typing `vi`, neither Tab nor the arrows do anything, "хотя до этого работало".
4. Erasing the line leaves an empty panel hanging, footer only.

## Root cause

Three of the four are one defect: ZERO CANDIDATES IS INVISIBLE.

`~/Downloads` holds exactly one entry, a file, and `cd` filters to directories — so the list
was empty and the key was swallowed in silence, indistinguishable from a broken feature. The
`vi` case is the same shape with a different source: confirmed as the late OSC 636 snapshot
race (the command provider has no names yet; the flaky TestBashSnapshotArrivesBeforeFirstPrompt
documents that window), and the arrows "stopped working" only because the dropdown never
opened, leaving them ordinary caret movement. The empty panel is the other side: the surface
stayed open with no rows.

The fourth is presentation: the panel took the pane's width instead of its content's.

## Fixed by

An explicit Tab with nothing to offer opens a non-selectable row that says WHY — no match,
no subdirectories here, or the command snapshot has not arrived yet — dismissed by the next
keystroke or Esc, never selectable, Enter falls through to submit. An erased document closes
the panel, and the footer-only state is unreachable by test. The panel is content-sized and
caret-anchored. And an explicit Tab's open intent now survives the latency budget, while a
typing query's still does not: a dropdown must not flash open under the fingers, but a person
who pressed Tab asked for the list and will wait for it.

## Acceptance Criteria

In a directory holding only a file, `cd ` + Tab shows a row naming the reason rather than
nothing; erasing the line closes the panel; the panel is as wide as its longest row, not as
wide as the pane.
close_reason: Shipped in 690a54e, verified by the coordinator in a real browser: in a directory holding only a file, cd + Tab renders 'No subdirectories in this folder' instead of nothing; erasing the line closes the panel; the panel measures 320px against a 1352px pane. The vi case was confirmed as the late OSC 636 snapshot race rather than a provider or arbiter defect, and is now surfaced by a snapshot-pending row.

title: A secret you can use from the prompt, and one you cannot leak into history by accident
description:
Owner's idea, 2026-08-02: run a test `curl` using an API key straight from the prompt, and —
before the command is sent — notice a key in what was typed and offer to save it.

## Why the second half is not a nicety

History now records commands verbatim and completion offers them back. So
`curl -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-..."` typed once already lands in the store today and is
offered as a candidate tomorrow — exactly the way the e2e's own commands surfaced in the
owner's dropdown this afternoon, only worse. We shipped the recording and never shipped the
guard. Detection is that guard, and it stands alone.

## Part 1 — detection, marking, masking (build first)

The moment is ideal: the line is still ours — before the PTY, before argv, before the screen.

- Detect on the typed line: known prefixes (sk-, ghp_, github_pat_, xox[baprs]-, AKIA, ASIA,
  glpat-, JWT shape, `-----BEGIN * PRIVATE KEY`) plus an entropy heuristic for long opaque
  tokens. Precision matters more than recall — a false positive interrupts a person mid-flow.
- Offer to save into the vault and replace with a reference, one keystroke.
- CRUCIALLY, when the user declines: the entry is still marked `sensitive`, so per design §9
  it never becomes ghost text, never appears as a completion candidate, and never enters an
  AI context. Those fields exist already — `sensitivity` on the entry, `eligibleForGhostText`
  on the Candidate — and nothing sets them today.
- Mask the value in the rendered block: the block draws from our own `intent`, so this is ours
  to do.

## Part 2 — references and substitution

- A reference syntax in the line, highlighted as a reference rather than as text, resolved at
  submit through the vault's existing sec:v1:<provider>:<id> grammar (ADR-0016, ADR-0017).
- THE INVARIANT: the ledger stores the REFERENCE, never the resolved value. This is not only
  hygiene — it is what makes recall useful: a command carrying a reference moves to another
  machine and resolves that machine's secret, while a command carrying a pasted key is both
  dead and dangerous.
- Prefer env injection for tools that read their own variables (OPENAI_API_KEY, GITHUB_TOKEN,
  AWS_*); fall back to the literal argument otherwise.

## What must be written down and NOT promised

Substitution puts the value in the process's argv, and argv is visible to `ps` for every
process on the machine and is recorded by audit and sudo. No architecture of ours removes
that — it is how exec works. An environment variable is slightly better (/proc/<pid>/environ
is same-user only) and covers most CLIs, but not an arbitrary curl header.

What we CAN guarantee, and what the ADR must state plainly: the secret does not reach our
ledger, does not reach the shell's own history file (we write the line), does not remain on
screen in the block, and never enters a model context. Under the owner's stated threat model
— protect the files from being read directly, not from processes running as the same user —
that is sufficient. Stating it is the point; implying more would be the defect.

## Success Criteria

A user pastes an API key into the prompt and is offered to store it before pressing Enter;
declining still keeps that command out of ghost text, out of completion and out of any AI
context. A command written with a secret reference runs with the real value, and the command
that comes back from history a week later shows the reference — not the key.
acceptance_criteria:
A user runs a command carrying an API key and is offered to save it AFTER it has run — attached to the block that just finished, never interrupting composition, focus never leaving the editor. Accepting stores the value in the vault and rewrites the stored row to a {{secret:NAME}} reference. The command that comes back from history a week later shows the reference, not the key, and running it resolves the live value at submit.

AMENDED 2026-08-03, after the feature was used. Two clauses of the original criterion describe a product we deliberately did not build, and closing against them would be closing against fiction:

1. 'offered to store it BEFORE pressing Enter' — the pre-submit panel is deleted. It interrupted the one moment a person is thinking about the command rather than about key management. The offer now arrives with the block, the way a password manager offers after a form is submitted.

2. 'declining still keeps that command out of ghost text, out of completion and out of any AI context' — overruled by the owner on 2026-08-02: 'давай просто отдавать маскированное', no sensitivity flag and no suppression machinery. The masked text is served everywhere, which is the whole policy; the sensitivity fields stay unset and unused.

What is NOT promised, and is written into ADR-0021 with measurements: the shell's own history file DOES record the resolved line in bash, zsh and fish. The product says 'save for reuse', never 'protect'.

PROVEN BY: e2e/prompt-vault.spec.ts ('run a key -> receipt on the block -> saved -> survives a restart as the reference') against a real backend, plus internal/app/capture_acceptance_test.go over the real socket.
notes:
OWNER DECISION 2026-08-02 (the '@' picker is passive):
- '@' inserts an ordinary '@' and enters no mode; keystrokes keep going to the line and the picker only filters.
- Nothing matches -> it CLOSES silently. Deliberately the opposite of the completion dropdown's 'zero candidates is a state we show': Tab is an explicit request and silence in answer to a request is a defect, while '@' is a passive trigger and a panel that stays up on no-match becomes a modal mode. Do not unify the two.
- Space closes it. Esc closes it and leaves the '@' as text. Only Enter/Tab on a selected row inserts the reference.
- Consequence: user@host and email addresses are safe even if the word-start rule ever lets one through — continuing to type closes it.
close_reason:
Closed against the AMENDED criterion (see the issue): the offer arrives after the command has run, attached to its block; saving stores the value and rewrites the row to a reference; a recalled command shows the reference and resolves the live value at submit. Two clauses of the original criterion described a product we deliberately did not build — the pre-submit panel and the sensitivity/suppression machinery — and both amendments are recorded with their reasons.

PROVEN: e2e/prompt-vault.spec.ts passes against a real backend (run a key -> receipt on the block -> saved -> restart -> recall gives the reference -> unlock -> runs with the live value). internal/app/capture_acceptance_test.go covers the same arc over the real socket. Frontend 1766 tests / 100 files, go test -race clean, contracts and both CSS gates clean.

NOT PROMISED, measured and written into ADR-0021: bash 5.3, zsh 5.9 and fish 4.8 all record the resolved line in their own history file. The product says 'save for reuse', never 'protect'.

Left open deliberately: nocx-yf4j (files in the '@' picker — a different capability), nocx-esgs (the headless e2e path cannot run 13 specs, pre-existing).

title: Completion offers cd onto a file, labels everything history, and hides directories
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

Type `cd `, press Tab.

Observed (owner, 2026-08-02, with screenshots): every row labelled `history`, no directories
at all, one of the offered lines is `cd ./<a file>` — so the product offers cd onto a file —
no way to tell a file from a directory, and "даже папки не все показываются".

## Root cause

`providers.ts` made the path provider applicable only when the token already contained `/`,
`.` or `~`. After `cd ` (empty token) and after `cd Down` (a bare word) it did not run at
all, so history — whose candidates replace the WHOLE line — was the only answer. When it did
run (`cd ./`) it returned files and directories alike, because nothing told it that `cd`
takes directories.

A second defect found while fixing it: `fs.complete` reported `isDir` from the directory
entry type without following symlinks, so a symlink to a directory would have been filtered
out by the new dirs-only rule — and a typical home directory is full of them.

## Fixed by

The path provider runs in argument position including an empty token; a three-entry table
(cd, pushd, rmdir) filters to directories with a documented default of "both" — an unknown
command is never treated as directories-only; every other command RANKS directories above
files rather than filtering, so nothing is hidden where a file is legitimate; each row
carries a Directory/File kind; paths outrank whole-line history in argument position with
history capped; Tab cycles and Shift+Tab goes back; and fs.complete stats the symlink target,
falling back to the entry type on a broken link.

Deliberately not solved here: knowing what kind of argument an arbitrary command takes. There
is no cheap oracle — bash has no completion specification for `cd` (a builtin) and `rmdir`'s
is a function name that would have to be executed. The table is a placeholder for nocx-w7h.15,
which deletes it.

## Acceptance Criteria

In a directory holding two subdirectories, a symlink to a directory and a file: `cd ` + Tab
lists the three directories each marked Directory with a trailing slash and omits the file;
a second Tab moves to the next candidate and previews it; `cat ` + Tab lists all four with
the file marked File and the directories first.
close_reason: Shipped in 9545449 and verified by the coordinator in a real browser against a directory holding two subdirectories, a symlink to a directory and a file: cd + Tab lists all three directories (link-to-dir among them, so the symlink repair holds) and omits notes.txt, a second Tab moves the preview from alpha/ to beta/, and cat + Tab lists all four with the file marked File and directories first.

title: The e2e suite writes commands into the developer's real history — the build-tag profile the memory records was never built
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

Run the e2e suite on a developer machine, then read the real store:

    ~/.local/share/nocx/content.db  →  29 rows, 7 of them the suite's own

    "printf '\033]0;NAME-msboyp8u\007'"   (tab-title probe)
    "printf '\033]0;T2-msboyhwv\007'"
    "printf '\033]0;T1-msboyguf\007'"
    "printf 'MS-%s\n' 2"  / 1 / 0
    "sleep 3; echo PROBE"
    "echo こんにちは"                      (the IME spec)

Found on 2026-08-02 while verifying Tab completion: the history provider offered the
suite's tab-title probes as completions for `pri`, in a real terminal, from the owner's own
profile.

## Why this is open again

`bd recall lesson-nocx-measured-2026-08-01-cost-a` records the decision that fixed it:
"a guard that somebody has to REMEMBER to apply is not a guard… nocx now picks its profile
directory by build tag, nocx-dev unless -tags release, so there is nothing to pass and
nothing to forget."

That is not in the tree. `internal/app/app.go:161` calls `storage.NewOSPaths("nocx")` with a
literal, there is no build-tagged app-name file in `internal/storage/`, and only the specs
that opt into `e2e/harness.ts`'s XDG dirs are isolated. The decision was recorded and never
built, so every spec that launches devharness without overriding XDG lands on the real
profile.

The blast radius grew today: before history recorded, the damage was settings and vault
state; now it is the developer's command history, which is also the completion provider's
corpus and the recall panel's content.

Corollary from the same memory, and the reason this stays invisible: a CI runner's $HOME is
fresh and disposable, so this defect is green in CI by construction. When a test touches
user state, ask where that state lives on a DEVELOPER's machine, never on the runner's.

## Acceptance Criteria

The default is safe with nothing to pass and nothing to forget: a debug build writes to a
dev profile directory, and only a release build uses the real one. A test asserts the
isolation holds — it fails if a run touches the real profile path — rather than a convention
each new spec must remember. The junk rows already in the owner's store are removed.
close_reason: Fixed on main by nocx-ti8w, merged here in 736517c: internal/storage/appdir.go plus build-tagged appdir_dev.go / appdir_release.go, so a dev build resolves nocx-dev and only -tags release resolves nocx; the e2e home boundary is now applied to every launcher, with a spec asserting it holds. The rows and the zzz-e2e-cmp-* files already written into the owner's release profile still need clearing — that part is a leftover, not a defect in the fix.

title: Search over commands: the filter, the coverage line, the detail pane
description:
The owner's ask, 2026-08-02: finish the block — completion and search. This is the search
half, scoped to what can actually be built today.

nocx-ms7v.2 (FTS across intent AND DERIVED TEXT) cannot be built yet: derived text is an
artifact, artifacts are schema v1 (nocx-rtg0.2), and output is not persisted at all today.
Searching commands is buildable now and is most of the value.

## Scope

- history.query gains a `text` filter: case-insensitive substring over `command`, applied
  within the rung the caller asked for. The frontend seam already sends it (8c73078) and
  the session-ledger fallback already filters the same way.
- No FTS. A substring match over a command column cannot use an index, and at history sizes
  that is fine and measurable; FTS arrives with output search, where the indexing unit is
  still an open decision (nocx-ms7v.7). Say this in the code rather than discovering it.
- The recall overlay gains a filter: typing narrows, the scope ladder still widens, and the
  existing source label still tells the truth about store vs session.
- A detail pane for the selected row — exit code, cwd, duration, when it last ran. Warp's
  equivalent is the reference; ours has the data already.
- COVERAGE (nocx-ms7v.3's requirement, folded in because it is one line of result and a lie
  without it): the result states how far back the store can see, so a search under a 30-day
  retention does not silently present a partial answer as the whole one.

## Deliberately out

Kind filter chips (Warp shows history/prompts/workflows/notebooks). We have exactly one
kind, and a filter that filters nothing is a lie about what the product holds. They arrive
with the second kind.

## Acceptance Criteria

Typing in the recall overlay narrows the rows to substring matches, case-insensitively, and
the rung ladder still widens from directory to host to everywhere. The result states its
coverage, and a search whose window is bounded by retention says so rather than showing a
partial answer as complete. The selected row shows exit code, cwd, duration and when it last
ran. Proven over the real socket, not against a fixture.
close_reason: Shipped in 970747f + 2cacd2b. Filter is a case-insensitive instr() within the rung (never LIKE — no wildcard grammar over the user's text), no FTS with the reason measured (~260us over 100k rows), coverage stated store-wide, detail pane with exit code/cwd/duration/last-ran, the kit's SearchField grown a display form rather than a hand-rolled input, matches bolded, and Enter inserts rather than executes whenever a filter is typed. Verified by the coordinator in a real browser: typing narrows to one row, the match is bold, and the first Enter left the block count unchanged.

title: AI dialogues are their own data class: retention, taint, and whether erasure means anything
description:
Raised by the owner twice ("осложняется тем, что мы записываем не только команды, но и вывод,
а в будущем еще и AI диалоги") and left open by ADR-0019 and ADR-0020, which both name it as
not decided.

A dialogue is not a command line. It holds far more incidental secret material — pasted
config, error text, file contents the agent read — and the user's expectation of "delete my
AI history" is much stronger than for a shell history.

What has to be decided:

- Its own setting and its own retention age, separate from command history. Today there is
  neither, and history.outputEnabled (Default: true) governs a capture path that does not
  exist.
- Sensitivity is a TAINT, not a flag. An agent answer derived from a secret-bearing artifact
  can disclose the secret while carrying sensitivity=normal itself. Propagation must be
  conservative and derivable from the provenance edges ADR-0019 §6 already requires.
- Redacted derivatives: what recall and search may hold for a dialogue whose evidence is
  sensitive.
- Whether erasure has to be real. A DELETE leaves rows in free space and WAL pages (this is
  already stated honestly in the retention copy). If "delete my AI history" must mean the
  bytes are unreadable, dialogues need their own key so crypto-erasure is possible without
  rewriting the whole content store. This trades against ADR-0018's deliberately narrow
  threat model (the detached copy) — the owner's scope call, not a default.

## Acceptance Criteria

An ADR records the decision on all four points, and the Settings surface either offers a
dialogue retention control that governs something real, or offers nothing at all — never a
control over a path that does not exist.

title: The context row above the prompt: environment as chips, each one a facet
description:
From the owner's Warp screenshot, 2026-08-02: above the prompt sits a row of chips — a JS glyph with 'v22.23.1', a folder with '~/Documents/repos/nocx', a branch glyph with 'main', and a file glyph with '7 • +369 -3' (changed files, insertions, deletions).

This is the epic's thesis made visible: identity is per-facet, so it renders per-facet. A single string could not say 'I know the cwd and the branch but not the runtime', and this row can — by leaving that chip out.

Two things it must not become. It is not a status line assembled from whatever we happen to know; each chip is a facet with its own confidence, and one at confidence=unknown is not rendered as a confident value (nocx-w7h.3 makes the same point for candidates). And the diff chip means we are reading the git working tree — decide deliberately how often and at what cost, because a repository with a large tree turns a decorative chip into a stall on every prompt.
acceptance_criteria: A row above the command line shows the environment as separate chips — runtime version, cwd, git branch, working-tree diff — each labelled by its own icon. A facet that is not known is ABSENT or shown as unknown; none of them is ever guessed. In a remote or nested environment a chip that describes the local machine does not appear. The chips come from the kit, and the row is a kit component, not markup drawn inside the terminal surface.

title: Tab at the prompt moves the focus out of the editor
description:
Tab is unbound in the editor — the editor installs no CM6 keymap at all (a comment in editor.ts says the keymap is a later wave's job) and CodeMirror's default keymap deliberately omits Tab for accessibility. So Tab was the browser's ordinary focus-move.

Measured in a real browser on 2026-08-02: typing 'ec' at the prompt and pressing Tab left the document unchanged and moved document.activeElement from .cm-content to nothing, so the next keystroke went nowhere. In a terminal, where Tab means completion, that is worse than doing nothing — the user gets no completion AND loses the prompt.

Swallowed for now, with a comment pointing at nocx-w7h.2 / .3 / nocx-4ff.23. Doing nothing is not the end state, it is the honest one until Tab has something to complete with.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Type a partial command at the prompt.
2. Press Tab.
3. Nothing completes, and the prompt no longer has the focus.
acceptance_criteria: Tab at the command prompt keeps the focus in the editor. Ctrl+Tab and Cmd+Tab still reach the window. Replaced, not extended, when completion lands.
close_reason: Fixed in a275091: Tab is swallowed at the prompt (editor.ts:390) with a test asserting the keydown is cancelled and document.activeElement is untouched. Replaced, not extended, when completion lands — nocx-4ff.23.

title: Rebuild the Export / Backup / Import page around one backup and one restore
description: Owner, 2026-08-02: 'Та страница устарела, ее нужно переделывать.' It is 649 lines offering configuration export, portable encrypted export with its own passphrase fields, a plaintext reveal, three separate import inputs (.json, .enc, Tabby .yml) and an 'include private content' checkbox whose content — conversations and command history — did not exist when it was written and now does. It grew as each capability landed, so it reads as a list of file formats rather than as the two verbs anyone actually wants.
acceptance_criteria: The section presents the two things a user came to do — make a backup, restore one — instead of an inventory of file formats. Every control on it does something that works today; a format we no longer produce is gone rather than hidden. Built from the kit (frontend/src/ui/), with no controls drawn inside the surface.
close_reason: Landed in 207aaab: page rebuilt around make-a-backup and restore-one, verified as a real-browser round trip

title: Restore re-keys the content database for the machine it lands on
description:
The content key is derived from the machine (nocx-rtg0.14), so raw ciphertext does not travel. That is deliberate: moving to another machine is what backup and restore are for. This bead is where the promise is kept.

Note the tension to resolve explicitly rather than by accident: the backup must be readable on B, so it cannot be encrypted under A's machine key — it is encrypted under the passphrase the user gives when making it (the section already has a 'portable encrypted export' with a passphrase). So the passphrase protects the backup, and the machine key protects the live database, and neither substitutes for the other.
acceptance_criteria: A backup made on machine A restores on machine B and its command history is readable there: the restore re-encrypts content.db under B's own key rather than copying ciphertext B cannot open. Restoring onto the SAME machine also works, and neither path re-mints a key for a database that already has one. A backup carries no machine-bound material — a copy of the backup on a third machine is as unreadable as a copy of content.db.

title: Take your terminal to a new machine
description:
The end-to-end check IS the epic: back up on A, restore on B, everything works. It is written here at creation because by the end we would know what the code does, and that is exactly the knowledge that produces a test the implementation passes.

The pieces exist and have never been exercised together: internal/export writes a backup through SQLite's online backup API, the Settings screen has an Export / Backup / Import section, and there are open bugs saying import is non-transactional (nocx-hdwh) and drops what export promised to carry (nocx-ojxa). Nobody has restored a backup on a second machine.

Restore is also the answer to a consequence recorded in nocx-rtg0.14: the content key is derived from the machine, so a raw copy of content.db opens on the old laptop and not the new one. That is correct and deliberate — moving a machine is what restore is for, and restore re-keys the database under the new machine rather than copying ciphertext. Migration is this epic's job, not the key's.
acceptance_criteria: On machine A you make one backup. On machine B you restore it, and your connections, groups, settings, secrets and command history are all there and usable — the SSH profile connects, the setting reads back, pressing Up answers with a command you ran on A and the panel says source=store. Restore is transactional: a failure at any step leaves the machine as it was, never half-imported. Deliberately out: continuous sync between two live machines, and any server-side component.

title: The unlock prompt exists on one path only: the backend cannot ask for it
description:
Root cause, found 2026-08-02 by reading the seam: the unlock prompt is raised in exactly ONE place — dispatcher.onVaultSealed in frontend/src/dispatcher.ts — and it fires when a JSON-RPC RESPONSE reports the vault sealed, deferring the caller's promise and retrying once. That design is right for anything the renderer initiates, and it is why no call site wraps its own vault calls.

Its blind spot is everything else. Work that needs the vault but did not begin as a renderer RPC raises no prompt at all and fails silently: the content key is read in app.New(), in Go, at startup, with no call, no renderer, and possibly no window. Any future backend-initiated work has the same hole. So the symptom 'the prompt appears sometimes' is really 'there is one path that prompts, and everything off it fails quietly'.

The fix is a second direction, not a patch on the first: the backend must be able to REQUEST an unlock (a server-to-client notification naming why it needs one), which the renderer turns into the same dialog through the same code. Then history at startup, and anything like it later, is covered by construction.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Let the vault seal (or start with it sealed).
2. Reach a surface that needs a secret — the prompt appears.
3. Now restart with history enabled: the content key read at startup needs the vault too, and nothing is ever shown.
acceptance_criteria: Every call path that reads or writes a secret through a sealed vault raises the unlock prompt; when it cannot (no UI attached, a provider that is unavailable, a prompt already open) it reports that to the caller and the surface shows it. No path returns success, an empty result, or silence. Proven per path, including the ones reached from a background refresh rather than from a click.

title: Every epic proves its happy path — the rule, and the audit of epics that never had one
description: Written after nocx-rtg0 shipped a store, a key, a budget, a policy, a wire method and five settings controls while ContentDB.Add had no caller — every gate green, feature absent. The rule is in AGENTS.md under 'Every epic proves its happy path'. What remains is applying it backwards: the other open epics were created under the old bar and most likely have the same hole.
acceptance_criteria: AGENTS.md carries the rule (done); and every open non-chore epic either names one end-to-end check in the user's words or is relabelled a chore. The audit names, per epic, the check and whether it exists today.

title: The app must say when a feature its settings advertise is not running
description:
Failing soft was the right call: a terminal that refuses to start because a key would not open is worse than one that starts without history. But the soft failure is a slog.Warn, and the Settings screen goes on offering a keep-history toggle, a retention age and a two-number budget, all of which govern nothing. A silent degrade that the UI contradicts is how a broken feature survives a release.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Start on a machine where the content key cannot be read.
2. Open Settings — History. Everything is there and none of it does anything.
acceptance_criteria: When durable history is unavailable, the History section says so where the user is looking — not only in a log line nobody reads — and the recall panel's source=session is surfaced rather than being indistinguishable from an empty store.

title: A field's size stops depending on what its caption happens to say
description:
Three things with one cause: something that only describes the control was allowed to size it, or to be measured as if it were one.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Open Settings → History with 'Keep history for' at 0: the field is wider than the two below it, because its caption is longer.
2. Type 1: the field shrinks as the caption becomes the shorter range.
3. Watch the console on mount: 'unusable value and default for setting history.enabled, got boolean, defaultType boolean' for every toggle.
acceptance_criteria: A number field's box is the same width and height whatever its caption says — the range, a sentinel's meaning, or an out-of-range error; every number field in a column is one width; and mounting a page of toggles logs nothing.
close_reason: Landed in 980dc2a; measured in a real browser

title: A sentinel value says what it means on the screen, not in the prose
description: Owner's verdict on 'Keep history for = 0': совсем неочевидно. Age expiry is opt-in by design — growth is bounded by the size budget instead — which makes 0 the value most people see, so it is the one value that must explain itself.
acceptance_criteria: NumberSpec declares ZeroLabel — what 0 means when 0 is a sentinel rather than a quantity — and it travels on the wire beside the unit and the bounds; while the value is 0 the caption slot reads that meaning instead of the range, at the quiet caption tone (0 is valid, not an error), and returns to the range as soon as the value is an ordinary number; the description no longer explains 0.
close_reason: Landed in 7243287; verified in a real browser

title: Double-click in a frozen block selects and copies the whole token
description:
The browser's native word segmentation stops at '-' and '.', and the earlier fix expanded the selection after the browser had already made one — so copy-on-select fired on mouseup with the first word only. The interception moves to mousedown with detail===2 and preventDefault() first, mirroring xterm.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run a command that prints a filename such as profile-usage.json.
2. Double-click the filename in the frozen block.
3. Only 'profile' is selected, then the selection visibly widens — and the clipboard holds 'profile'.
acceptance_criteria: A double-click on 'profile-usage.json' in a frozen block selects the whole token, and copy-on-select puts the whole token on the clipboard — not the first word and not a later expansion of it; the selection is applied once, before the browser makes its own, the way xterm's SelectionService does it.
close_reason: Landed in 722db2e; verified in a real browser against the dev stand

title: The selected recall row stays fully visible while walking a rung taller than the panel
description:
scrollIntoView({block:'nearest'}) resolved the row against the wrong scroller — the panel floats over the scrollback — and never un-straddles a partially visible row. The reveal is computed from live rects against the list itself, after the footer is laid out.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Build more history than the panel can show.
2. Press Up to open recall — the selected row is clipped by the list's bottom edge.
3. Hold Up to the top — the selection jumps to the end and will not walk back.
acceptance_criteria: With more rows than fit, the row selected on open is fully inside the list box; every Up and Down keeps the selected row fully inside it; reaching the top does not jump the selection to the far end, and Down walks back the way it came.
close_reason: Landed in 722db2e; verified in a real browser against the dev stand

title: Cmd/Ctrl+V reaches the command editor from anywhere in the pane
description:
Focus-only by design — the keydown is left uncancelled so the browser dispatches its paste event at the now-focused editor, rather than reading the clipboard here and bypassing CM6.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Copy some text.
2. Click a frozen command block, so the focus leaves the editor.
3. Press Cmd/Ctrl+V — nothing is pasted.
acceptance_criteria: With the focus on a frozen block or the scrollback, Cmd/Ctrl+V focuses the editor and the clipboard text is inserted at the caret by CM6's own paste path; the literal \x16 never reaches the shell; a settings field, quick connect or a dialog keeps its own paste.
close_reason: Landed in 722db2e; verified in a real browser against the dev stand

title: Escape reaches the editor after a click moved the focus out of it
description:
The editor's capture listener only sees keys that traverse its own surface, so after a click elsewhere Escape never reached it and the draft survived — which reads as 'Esc does nothing'. Same rescue policy as the typing path in TerminalContent.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Type a draft into the command editor.
2. Click a frozen command block above it, so the focus leaves the editor.
3. Press Escape — the draft is still there.
acceptance_criteria: With the editor on screen but the focus elsewhere in the pane (a frozen block, the scrollback, the chrome), Escape clears the draft; with the recall overlay open it dismisses the overlay and restores the captured draft rather than clearing it; somebody else's text control, a modal overlay and the block action menu all keep their own Escape.
close_reason: Landed in 722db2e; verified in a real browser against the dev stand

title: A number setting shows its unit and its range without a second vocabulary
description: The allowed-range hint was a floating span the settings surface drew for itself, left of the control, and the unit was explained in prose inside each description. Owner's call: unit beside the value, range beneath the field, always visible, smaller type, right-aligned. Everything a consumer other than the screen needs (unit, bounds) is declared once in the registry.
acceptance_criteria: The unit ('days','MiB') is declared in NumberSpec beside Min/Max and travels on the wire; the settings screen renders it as a suffix inside the control and the range as a permanent caption beneath the field, right-aligned with the field's column; an out-of-range value replaces the caption in the same slot without changing the field's height; the backend's own rejection is not repeated underneath when the caption already says it, while an unpredicted rejection still reaches the user verbatim.
close_reason: Landed in 722db2e; verified in a real browser against the dev stand

title: Shell integration writes ~/.nocx and the user's rc files from every build, including test runs
description:
Found while verifying the claim that a development build no longer touches the
developer's home (nocx-ti8w step 1).

internal/app/app.go:200 calls ShellIntegration.EnsureInstalled(home) on every
App.Start(), with home from os.UserHomeDir(). That writes ~/.nocx
(internal/shellintegration/scripts.go:26, dirName = ".nocx") and appends a
sourcing gate to the user's shell rc files. It goes through neither
storage.Paths nor DocumentStore, so the build-tag profile split does not cover
it: a dev backend, a devharness and every e2e run still write the developer's
real home on startup.

For an installed app this is correct and is the feature. For a test run it is
the same class of defect as nocx-ti8w — user state written by a process that
only exists to be tested — and it is the more damaging half, because rc files
are hand-edited and an append is not idempotent by construction the way a
document write is.

Blast radius is every spec: EnsureInstalled runs from Start(), not from any
particular RPC.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Remove ~/.nocx and note the tail of ~/.bashrc.
2. Start any nocx backend built from this repo — `make dev-web` is enough.
3. ~/.nocx exists again and the rc gate has been (re-)appended, from a build
   that resolves the nocx-dev profile for everything else.

## Acceptance Criteria

The home directory the shell integration installs into is injected rather than
resolved inside Start(), so an e2e or dev composition can point it at the
isolated root. A test asserts that a backend composed for tests writes no file
outside that root — including ~/.nocx and rc files.
close_reason: Superseded rather than dropped. The defect is real — app.go:200 writes ~/.nocx and appends to rc files on every Start(), from every build — but the fix it specified (inject the home into App) is both more work and less coverage than the HOME boundary now planned as nocx-ti8w step 2, which neutralises ~/.nocx, the rc files, ~/.ssh/config and the config dir at once and needs no production change. Reopen if step 2 lands in a form that leaves the shell-integration write uncovered.

title: The e2e suite runs against the real ~/.config/nocx and resets your settings to defaults
description:
Measured 2026-08-01 while debugging a report that the UI theme reverts on its own.

The default e2e fixture in e2e/harness.ts (the `test` export, lines 30-61) does nothing
but shim the two Wails bindings. It sets no environment, so the backend the suite drives
resolves storage.NewOSPaths("nocx") to the developer's real ~/.config/nocx. The ONLY XDG
isolation anywhere in the repo is VaultBackend in that same file (lines 127-134,
XDG_CONFIG_HOME/DATA/CACHE), used by the vault specs — the pattern exists and was simply
never applied to the default path.

Specs that write the live settings document as a matter of course:
  theme-switch.spec.ts:26,43,86,104  ui.theme -> light, dracula, ends on tokyo-night
  proof-matrix.spec.ts:356,382       ui.theme -> light, ends on tokyo-night
  tabs.spec.ts:61,264                tab.placement, ends on horizontal
  focus-after-reorder.spec.ts:15     tab.placement
  vertical-tab-placement.spec.ts:21  tab.placement

So a developer picks a theme, someone runs the suite — themselves or an agent in another
worktree — and the theme is silently back to tokyo-night. It needs no second app window:
the suite brings its own backend.

theme-switch.spec.ts:103 states the assumption out loud: "Leave the app on the default so
a shared-state run does not inherit it." The cleanup writes the DEFAULT, not the value
that was there before, which is correct against an isolated dir and destructive against a
live one.

nocx-z069 (closed) moved dev-web off the e2e port precisely so a dev stand and a suite run
could be up at the same time. That made the shared config directory a live hazard rather
than a theoretical one.

The fix is isolation at the runner, not restore-in-spec: restoring in each spec cannot
cover the wails dev path and re-introduces the bug on every new spec. Related but
distinct: nocx-h2gf (two backends lose each other's writes) is the general
last-writer-wins defect; this bead is the specific reason a developer sees it every day.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the app (or `make dev-web`) and set Settings -> Interface -> Theme to anything
   other than Tokyo Night. Confirm ~/.config/nocx/settings.json now holds that value.
2. Run the e2e suite, or just `npx playwright test e2e/theme-switch.spec.ts`.
3. Read ~/.config/nocx/settings.json again: ui.theme is back to "tokyo-night".
   The same run leaves tab.placement on "horizontal".

## Acceptance Criteria

Every e2e path (headless devharness and wails dev) runs against an isolated config/data/
cache dir, so a suite run cannot read or write the developer's live ~/.config/nocx.
Proved by a test that records the live settings document before a run and asserts it is
byte-identical afterwards.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text: The XDG trick VaultBackend uses is Linux-only, so the fix cannot be 'copy those three env lines into the default fixture'. internal/storage/paths.go:73-87 newDarwinPaths never reads XDG — it goes straight to os.UserHomeDir() and returns ~/Library/Application Support/nocx. macOS is the product's primary platform, which means the vault specs believe they are isolated and on a Mac are writing the developer's real Application Support directory. Whatever mechanism this bead lands must isolate identically on both platforms, and the absence must not be silent.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
Blast radius, measured: 22 of the 25 spec files run against the developer's real config dir. Only vault.spec.ts, vault-settings.spec.ts and tabby-import.spec.ts construct isolated XDG dirs via VaultBackend. So it is not only settings — every non-vault spec drives a backend whose profiles.json, vault.json and vault-file.json are the developer's real ones.

Design input from an independent review (codex, read-only): the fix must be fail-closed composition, not a test-mode boolean. A runtime flag that selects an in-memory store fails exactly the same way this bug did — forget to pass it and app.go:101/105/108 still construct production paths, the real DocumentStore and the real keychain provider. Required shape instead: remove NewOSPaths from app.New (production main resolves it, the shared constructor takes an explicit required Dependencies struct with no nil fallback); a build-tagged e2e entry point that has no code path to production paths at all; mandatory --state-dir with a runner-created sentinel token; canonicalised root validation (reject the real home, symlinked roots, pre-existing dirs without the sentinel); the system keychain provider not registered at all in ordinary e2e rather than merely defaulted away.

Also flagged, and out of the current title's scope: storage is not the only home-derived capability the composition root takes — app.go:87 reads ~/.ssh/config. 'The test backend cannot touch the developer's home' is not established by fixing DocumentStore alone.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
APPROVED PLAN (owner, 2026-08-01), after comparing tabby / termic / orca:

tabby has no tests at all, so it is not a model. termic puts the primary defence in the BUILD, not in a flag: src-tauri/src/lib.rs:555 'const APP_DIR = if cfg!(debug_assertions) { "termic_dev" } else { "termic" }', with TERMIC_DATA_DIR as a second layer that is deliberately dead in release. orca redirects HOME/USERPROFILE/app.getPath('home') into a disposable dir, ASSERTS that isolation in tests/e2e/electron-home-isolation.spec.ts, and runs a tripwire that watches the real ~/.codex for writes without reading contents.

The lesson both my proposal and the codex review missed: safety must not depend on remembering to pass something. nocx today resolves the SAME directory for wails dev, devharness, e2e and release.

Order of work:
1. Split the dev and release directories by build tag (nocx-dev vs nocx), the way termic's APP_DIR does. Small, inside internal/storage, no flag to forget, and on its own it stops the dev stand and the suite touching the release profile. The unsafe direction must be the one that needs the explicit tag: forgetting it yields the dev profile, never the user's.
2. Explicit --state-dir / env override, alive only in dev builds, for a per-run or per-worker scratch profile. Required if e2e ever goes parallel (termic runs maxInstances:1 precisely because they could not inject per-worker dirs).
3. A test that asserts the isolation holds, orca-style. This is the check that was missing: the mechanism existed and was simply not applied.
4. A tripwire over the real config dir during e2e — detect a breach rather than trust the wiring.
5. Keychain, per the codex review: dev composition registers the file provider only; system.New() is not constructed at all.

Not urgent, still right: the app.New(Dependencies) composition refactor from the codex review. Step 1 does not need it.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
Step 1 landed on branch fix/dev-release-profile-split-nocx-ti8w (3efc054): the profile directory is now chosen by the build tag — nocx-dev for every build, nocx only under -tags release. Verified by running the resolver in both modes: ~/.config/nocx-dev vs ~/.config/nocx. A real devharness started from this branch created nothing under the release profile. Full pre-commit gate green.

Bead stays OPEN: its acceptance criterion is per-run isolation and an assertion test, and neither is met yet. Remaining, in order: (2) explicit per-run --state-dir, dev builds only — required before e2e can go parallel, since make dev-web and a concurrent suite run now share nocx-dev and still clobber each other; (3) an orca-style test asserting the isolation actually holds; (4) tripwire over the release profile during e2e; (5) dev composition registers the file vault provider only, so the OS keychain — which is reached outside the DocumentStore seam — stops being shared.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
PLAN REVISED after reading orca's actual implementation (tests/e2e/helpers/electron-home-isolation.ts, 116 lines) rather than describing it from memory. The owner was right to push back: orca solves this with ONE boundary, and it answers the objection I used to dismiss HOME redirection.

What it does: HOME/USERPROFILE/HOMEDRIVE/HOMEPATH point at <userDataDir>/home; every restricted key is STRIPPED from the inherited env before the isolated ones are set, so a leaked variable cannot survive; a caller passing any restricted key in launchEnv/extraEnv gets an exception rather than a silent override; the root is canonicalised with realpathSync.native (the symlink hole codex flagged); launch is refused if the isolated home equals the real one; and a post-launch assertion verifies the app actually resolved it, without printing the real path into CI artifacts.

The part that changes our design: ZDOTDIR, ORCA_ORIG_ZDOTDIR, BASH_ENV and ENV are in the restricted set. That is the answer to 'but the PTY spawns the user's login shell and reads their rc files', which is exactly why I had proposed per-capability injection instead.

So step 2 becomes: one HOME boundary for every backend the suite launches, orca-style, rather than a per-run --state-dir. It covers ~/.config/nocx, ~/.nocx, the rc files and ~/.ssh/config in one place with NO production code change, and it works on macOS, where XDG_CONFIG_HOME does not (newDarwinPaths resolves os.UserHomeDir(), which honours $HOME; os.UserConfigDir() likewise).

This subsumes nocx-q2zx, which should be closed as covered rather than implemented as specified. It does NOT subsume step 5: the OS keychain is not home-derived on either platform, and orca does not solve that either. Step 1 (the build-tag split) also stands on its own — it protects interactive make dev-web, which has no fixture at all.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
Step 2 partially landed on branch feat/e2e-home-boundary-nocx-ti8w (c1ff2a3): e2e/home-isolation.ts plus five assertions, wired into playwright.config.ts's wails dev webServer — the default path and CI's.

Honest scope of what is now true: the boundary is proved to be HANDED OVER, not proved to be OBEYED. assertResolvedIsolatedHome is written and has no caller, and the wails dev path could not be exercised locally (this machine has no GTK/display), so it is verified by reading rather than by running. VaultBackend still isolates by XDG (Linux-only) rather than by home. The headless path builds its backend outside Playwright and is untouched.

Remaining, in order: (a) a live assertion that a launched backend resolved the isolated home — cheapest reliable signal is <isolatedHome>/.nocx appearing, since App.Start() installs shell integration on every launch, which is both the proof and the write that was doing the damage; (b) VaultBackend takes a home instead of the XDG trio, which also simplifies its three callers, since an isolated HOME makes the XDG dirs redundant on Linux and works on macOS where they do not; (c) the headless path must fail loudly when the boundary is absent rather than run unisolated; (d) step 5, the keychain, which no home boundary reaches on either platform.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
Steps 2 and 3 complete on branch feat/e2e-home-boundary-nocx-ti8w (c1ff2a3, 7d2982e). Boundary applied to both launchers the suite owns: playwright.config.ts for wails dev, VaultBackend for the specs that start their own devharness (its three callers migrated from the XDG trio to a disposable root). The headless path, which builds its backend outside Playwright, is now refused by e2e/preflight.ts unless the runner exports NOCX_E2E_HOME_DIR — red until adopted, deliberately.

Proved obeyed, not just handed over: a real devharness started behind the boundary installs ~/.nocx INSIDE the disposable home, and a run without the boundary leaves that home with zero entries, so the assertion has teeth. 12 assertions green on both browsers.

Found while checking the test could fail: the companion real-home mtime check is near-vacuous, because EnsureInstalled is version-gated and reinstalling the same version does not move the mtime. Left in as a labelled tripwire rather than removed, with the limitation written next to it.

REMAINING, and it is the last item: step 5, the OS keychain. system.New() is constructed unconditionally at app.go:108, reached outside the DocumentStore seam, and home-derived on neither platform — so nothing landed here touches it. An ordinary e2e composition must stop registering the system provider at all rather than merely defaulting away from it.

Also unverified by running rather than reading: the wails dev path, because this machine has no GTK or display. CI exercises it on macos-latest.

title: Shell integration scripts ship to nobody when `version` is not bumped
description:
## Context

`EnsureInstalled` writes ~/.nocx/shell-integration.bash only when the installed VERSION file differs from the `version` constant in scripts.go — that short-circuit runs before anything looks at the script's content. So a script edited without bumping the constant reaches no shell: every session keeps sourcing the copy installed the last time the number changed.

Found by the owner: the OSC 636 command-existence hook (nocx-w7h.6, 8d9408f) did nothing in the app. The backend binary carried the new 14210-byte script, go test passed, and ~/.nocx/shell-integration.bash was still the 6504-byte copy from 2026-07-26 because `version` was left at "7".

Nothing connected the script bytes to the number that governs their delivery, which is why two workers and one review all missed it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Edit internal/shellintegration/scripts/nocx.bash; leave `version` alone.
2. Rebuild and start the backend, open a new tab.
3. `grep 636 ~/.nocx/shell-integration.bash` — the edit is absent, and the app behaves as if the change was never made.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `version` is bumped to "8" so the OSC 636 script actually installs.
- A test hashes the embedded scripts and fails when they change without a version bump, printing the digest to record. Prove it fails: append a line to a script, run the test, see it fail; revert, see it pass.
- The failure message names the consequence (an installed VERSION is never rewritten), not just the mismatch.
close_reason: Bumped version to 8 in dfda66e and added TestScriptVersionTracksScriptContent, which hashes the embedded scripts and fails when they change without a bump. Proven to fail by appending a line to nocx.bash and reverting.

title: The command line says whether the command exists — local bash first
description:
## Context

Owner, three times, with evidence. The last: `sdfsdf` renders green in the input line
before Enter, and `dssdfdsf` ran to `exit 127`. Green now carries ZERO information — it
means "you typed a word first". The old 67-word dictionary at least meant "one of these
67". We traded an arbitrary signal for no signal, which is honest and useless.

zsh-syntax-highlighting solves this by living INSIDE zsh: it reads the live tables of
aliases, functions, builtins, hashed and external commands. We cannot, because ADR-0004
gives our editor the line and the shell never sees it until submit. So we must ask.

Not a daemon. Warp ships a 215 MB remote-server binary (measured: 622 MB and three
processes on this box). We need a list of names, not an agent.

## Scope — deliberately the smallest honest loop

LOCAL BASH ONLY. Prove the whole path end to end on the machine the owner tests on, then
widen to zsh and remote. Do not build per-shell abstraction layers before there is a
second shell.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Type `sdfsdf` at the prompt. It renders as a command, identically to `ls`.
2. There is no way to tell, before Enter, that it does not exist.

## Design constraints — each one was argued and is not up for reinvention

- **Four states, and unavailable is NOT unresolved.** `resolved` (snapshot applies, name
  found), `unresolved` (snapshot applies, is fresh, literal name not found),
  `indeterminate` (expansion/substitution — no literal name to check), `unavailable` (no
  hook, no snapshot, or stale). On a host with no integration everything must render
  `unavailable`, never red — that would be the same lie in the other direction.
- **Not a red foreground.** Red reads as a guaranteed syntax error. Use a subtle underline
  so it reads as a diagnostic remark about one word.
- **The transport is the existing shell-integration hook.** It already emits OSC 133 and
  OSC 7 and already installs on remote hosts. Add a payload type, do not add a channel.
  Follow VS Code's OSC 633 shape, which is documented and in production: a private OSC
  code, typed sub-command letters, `Key=Value` properties with a whitelist on receive
  ("only known properties will be handled"), a nonce against forged sequences from command
  output, and `\xAB` hex escaping rather than base64.
- **Never blocks the prompt.** `compgen -c` is 37 ms here and can be seconds on NFS. The
  snapshot is computed after the prompt is usable, never in front of it.
- **Advisory only.** It never gates submission, never weakens a confirmation, never
  participates in a security decision. Any process can print our OSC.
- **The frozen headers keep their verdict from submit time.** Yesterday's `deploy` must not
  turn red today because the script was deleted.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `pwd` (a bash builtin, not a file — so PATH alone would answer wrong) renders resolved.
- `sdfsdf` renders unresolved, with an underline rather than a red foreground.
- `$TOOL build` and `"$(pick)" arg` render indeterminate, never unresolved.
- With the hook absent, every command renders unavailable and nothing is underlined.
- The prompt appears without waiting for the snapshot — asserted, not assumed.
- Output that prints our OSC sequence cannot replace the snapshot (nonce enforced).
- The snapshot never reaches a log, a diagnostic bundle or ContentDB: the full alias and
  function list is a fingerprint of the user's working environment.
close_reason: OSC 636 command-existence layer landed in 8d9408f: private OSC with H/S sub-commands, per-session nonce, background compgen so the prompt never waits, per-tab store owned by XtermRenderer, four states with unavailable never collapsing into unresolved. Two defects found in review and fixed before commit: a module singleton that judged tab 2 against tab 1's command set, and a staging file named after the nonce (published it to ls /tmp and to ps via mv argv, and leaked on early exit).

title: Replace the shell dictionary with the VS Code grammar via Shiki
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start the app, wait for the prompt editor.
2. Type `ls` — it is coloured as a command.
3. Type `pwd` — it is NOT coloured.
4. Same divergence in a frozen block header after running each.

## Cause

@codemirror/legacy-modes shell mode colours commands from a hardcoded 67-word list
(commonCommands in shell.cjs): it has ls/cd/grep/make and lacks pwd/cargo/kubectl/docker
and every user script. Arbitrary and unexplainable to a user.

A positional rule of our own was considered and REJECTED as worse: it would colour the
typo `sdf` as a command, which is false precision, while the dictionary at least stays
silent. Silence is honest; a confident wrong answer is not.

## Fix, verified by actually running it

Shiki 4.4.1 with the VS Code shellscript TextMate grammar. Measured output for
`ls -la | grep foo > out.txt`, `pwd`, `cargo test`, `sdf dffd`:

- ls, pwd, cargo, sdf ALL get entity.name.command.shell — positional, no dictionary
- pwd additionally gets support.function.builtin.shell
- -la is constant.other.option.dash.shell, pipe is keyword.operator.pipe.shell,
  redirect is keyword.operator.redirect.shell, out.txt is string.unquoted.argument.shell

It makes NO existence claim, which is what keeps it honest.

- shiki/engine/javascript avoids Oniguruma WASM entirely — no CSP risk in the packaged app
- includeExplanation 'scopeName' returns SCOPE NAMES, not theme colours, so our --color-*
  semantic tokens keep owning the palette
- 0.23 ms per realistic line; the shellscript grammar is a standalone 45 KB module

## Sync vs async (owner, 2026-08-01)

Tokenisation stays SYNCHRONOUS. 0.23 ms is a seventieth of a frame; making it async buys
nothing and adds stale-result and flicker handling. Asynchrony belongs to the LATER
existence layer, where a verdict from the shell arrives after a round trip and must be
layered over already-painted structure rather than repainting it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- ls, pwd, cargo, kubectl, docker and ./scripts/release are styled identically as
  commands. No word is special.
- sdf is styled as a command too and carries NO existence diagnostic.
- Live editor and frozen block headers come from the same tokenizer call and cannot
  diverge.
- No colour literals; the colour and css-integrity linters stay green.
- The commonCommands dependency is gone from the codebase.
- The bundle delta is measured and reported, not estimated.
close_reason: Landed in c5aa4b7. The 67-word commonCommands dictionary is gone; @codemirror/legacy-modes is removed from package.json. Shiki 4.4.1 with the VS Code shellscript TextMate grammar, JS regex engine (no Oniguruma WASM, so no CSP question in the packaged app), scope names via includeExplanation so our --color-* tokens keep the palette. ls, pwd, cargo, kubectl, docker, ./scripts/release AND sdf all resolve to entity.name.command.shell — positional, no list, and no existence claim about any of them. One tokenizer feeds the live editor and the frozen headers so they cannot drift; scopes map to tok-* by innermost scope, longest prefix first. Synchronous by decision: 0.23ms is a seventieth of a frame; asynchrony belongs to the later existence layer, and no seams were built for it. Bundle 286.13 -> 325.58 kB gzip plus 41.48 kB grammar and 26.72 kB theme as async chunks. 1334 -> 1339 tests. NOT verified: the plain-then-decorate path before the grammar resolves (not deterministically exercisable) and per-line timing inside the app.
