title: Sandbox slice 4: pty/session/app/transport plumbing, open + sandbox.status + dialog.openDirectory contracts
description:
Plan: .internal/plans/2026-08-02-native-filesystem-sandbox-v1.md, Slice 4. Spec §4, §6-7.

pty.Config.Sandbox *sandbox.Request; session.Config.Sandbox passthrough; localPTYFactory gets injected sandbox.Service (composition root only, internal/app/app.go); NewLocal builds ordinary command first (exec.Command(shell,-i), Dir, env unchanged), calls Service.Prepare only when request non-nil. openParams.Sandbox; handleOpen validation: local-only, flag on (-32010 feature-disabled), canonicalize workspace (Abs -> EvalSymlinks -> Stat; single canonical value as cmd.Dir + policy input + response metadata; invalid -> -32602). Result gains sandbox:{backend,workspace,writableRoots}; ordinary/SSH results omit it. sandbox.status method ({available,backend,reason?,detail?,abi?}). dialog.openDirectory + DialogService.OpenDirectory + contracts/dialog.openDirectory.schema.json + generated client type. title: Sandbox slice 2: strict Linux Landlock backend, helper, ABI probes, enforcement tests
description:
Plan: .internal/plans/2026-08-02-native-filesystem-sandbox-v1.md, Slice 2. Spec §8.

NewLinux(logger) Service. Helper: re-exec os.Executable() as __sandbox-landlock-exec before Wails startup; unlinked mode-0600 policy FD via ExtraFiles; readiness pipe (0=enforced, 1=typed failure, exit 126); PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS; strict RestrictPaths at min(detectedABI,8) from landlock.V8-equivalent set; NO BestEffort/RestrictNet/RestrictScoped; send success only after restriction; remove helper-only env; unix.Exec real shell without intermediate shell. ABI floor 3 -> landlock-abi-too-old below; probe failure -> landlock-unavailable. Bounded readiness timeout in pty path: close PTY, terminate+wait helper, cleanup once, -32012, no registry entry.

Add Makefile target sandbox-smoke-linux (named, modeled on conformance; runs loudly, not env-hidden).
acceptance_criteria: restrict_linux_test.go on ABI>=3 runner: create/truncate/rename inside each writable root; read system executables; sentinel outside roots unreadable/unwritable; no bypass via symlink/subprocess/renamed path; post-launch hard-link creation to outside files denied at link(2); pre-existing hard link inside a writable root stays reachable (documented limitation, asserted as limitation not guarantee); outbound TCP retained. Helper: FD round-trip, status byte only after restrict success, exit 126 on error, idempotent Close, no leaked helper.
close_reason: Slice 2 committed: Landlock backend + helper + enforcement smoke; hook gates green

title: Sandbox slice 1: internal/sandbox contracts, canonical policy builder, stubs, pure tests
description:
Plan: .internal/plans/2026-08-02-native-filesystem-sandbox-v1.md, Slice 1. Spec: .internal/specs/2026-08-02-native-filesystem-sandbox-design.md §5-7.

Create internal/sandbox: Request{Workspace}, Status{Available,Backend,Reason,Detail,ABI}, Policy (validated canonical doc, JSON-serializable, bounded), CommandSpec, PreparedCommand (idempotent Close), Service{Status,Prepare}. Policy builder: BuildPolicy + gitCommonDir (parse only selected roots .git gitdir: line; malformed -> no extra root, no error; no parent search; canonicalize). Root model: RW = workspace + git common dir + runtime home/tmp under storage CacheDir/sandbox-sessions/<random>/; RO = documented system set + canonical shell + existing canonicalized PATH dirs. Reject NUL/empty/relative/nonexistent/non-directory/failed-symlink/duplicate-conflicting/bound-exceeded. RW subsumes RO.

Landlock/darwin constructors are stubs in this slice (typed setup failures); sandbox_other.go is final (unsupported-platform). Add go.mod direct require github.com/landlock-lsm/go-landlock v0.9.0.

title: Native per-tab filesystem sandbox (opt-in, experimental) — V1 implementation
description:
Implement the opt-in, experimental, filesystem-only per-tab sandbox designed in .internal/specs/2026-08-02-native-filesystem-sandbox-design.md. Evidence: .internal/reports/2026-08-02-native-filesystem-sandbox-research.md. Decision: ADR-0019 (docs/decisions/0019-native-per-tab-filesystem-sandbox.md). Executable decomposition: .internal/plans/2026-08-02-native-filesystem-sandbox-v1.md (6 slices).

Contract: one default-off setting sandbox.enabled (Experimental, PublicConfig); Sandboxed shell… Quick Connect action + native workspace picker; internal/sandbox.Service behind landlock/seatbelt/unsupported backends; open gains sandbox:{workspace}; sandbox.status; dialog.openDirectory; reserved -32010/-32011/-32012; fail-closed launch; Landlock ABI floor 3 cap 8; macOS Seatbelt runtime-probed and release-smoke-gated; ordinary/SSH/initial tabs unchanged.
design: Backends: Linux Landlock via github.com/landlock-lsm/go-landlock v0.9.0 (strict min(detectedABI,8), no BestEffort/RestrictNet/RestrictScoped; helper re-exec with unlinked policy FD + readiness pipe). macOS: deterministic SBPL render + sandbox-exec -p <shell> -i, /usr/bin/true probe. Common filesystem policy: canonical workspace + optional Git common dir (.git gitdir:) + ephemeral CacheDir/sandbox-sessions/<random>/{home,tmp}; isolated HOME/XDG/TMPDIR; NOCX_SANDBOX=filesystem. Renderer requests {workspace} only; backend canonicalizes and owns policy.
acceptance_criteria: Six slices land green per plan: (1) internal/sandbox contracts+policy+stubs; (2) Linux Landlock backend + helper + enforcement tests; (3) macOS SBPL renderer + probe + release-artefact smoke; (4) pty/session/app/transport plumbing + wire contracts; (5) frontend picker/action/live-flag/metadata/errors; (6) regression e2e + packaging + release gates. Platform smoke proves behavior (create/truncate/rename in writable roots; sentinel outside roots unreadable; no symlink/subprocess/renamed-path bypass; post-launch hard-link creation denied; outbound TCP retained). Fail-closed: no unsandboxed fallback; no session registered before enforcement readiness.
notes: Reopened 2026-08-03 after review of PR #62: the epic's happy path ('open a filesystem-isolated local tab') does not hold. Verified on the dev host (NixOS): no sandboxed tab can launch at all; and on any distro '> /dev/null' inside the cage fails. Findings filed as children.

Adds as a GROUP in the same list, never a second level (the decision recorded on the epic), so it is additive by construction.

Browsing the cwd is NOT it — Tab already does that, and a second way to do one thing is the near-duplicate the kit rules exist to prevent.
close_reason: Superseded by nocx-yf4j — the same task, standalone. It is about FILES in the '@' picker, and the epic's success criterion is about secrets; it lived here only because the picker does. beads ids encode the parent, so detaching was not possible: recreated instead.

title: A secret in the prompt looks like a chip, and a pasted key offers to become one
description: Frontend round: CodeMirror atomic range decoration for the chip, the vault picker built from the kit (never a bespoke control inside the surface), and the offer-to-save. Blocked by the panels round because it touches frontend/src/ui and the editor.
acceptance_criteria: Typing a key into the prompt offers to store it before Enter; declining still keeps that command out of ghost text and completion. A stored reference renders as a named chip, not as {{...}}, and the vault picker inserts one without leaving the prompt.
close_reason: chip (atomic CM6 range), passive @ picker with grouped list and sealed/uninitialized offers, non-modal save offer, resolve-at-submit with the reference kept in the ledger, and the masked-row second door. Acceptance e2e passes end to end in the coordinator stand.

title: The completion adapter: a second shell in the same environment answers what only a shell knows
description:
Design spec §17.1 option 2, and the thing that deletes three workarounds at once. Raised by
the owner 2026-08-02 while asking how we decide that `cd` takes directories.

## What we can answer without it

Local paths (fs.complete reads the filesystem directly) and command names anywhere (the OSC
636 snapshot is the running shell's own `compgen -c`, so it is correct on a remote host).

## What no amount of local cleverness can answer

- Subcommands: `git ch` → checkout / cherry-pick. These are git's completion FUNCTIONS, not
  data we can carry.
- Dynamic completers: kubectl, docker, `npm run`, make targets.
- The user's own completions from their rc file.
- Remote paths, for a different reason: our backend's filesystem is not the remote one.
- "What kind of argument does this command take" — the question that forced the three-entry
  cd/pushd/rmdir table. Checked on 2026-08-02: bash has NO completion specification for `cd`
  (a builtin), and `rmdir`'s is `complete -F _comp_complete_longopt` — a function NAME, which
  would have to be executed to learn anything. There is no cheap oracle; there is only
  running the shell's own machinery.

## The shape

NOT the user's shell: ADR-0004 hands it the line atomically at submit, so its readline buffer
is empty or stale — that is why §8.7's "forward a raw tab" was withdrawn.

A SECOND shell in the same environment — the lane of ADR-0020. It receives the whole line
plus the caret offset, runs the shell's own completion machinery (`_completion_loader`, then
`compgen -F _git -- ch`), and returns candidates. The user's line is never touched.

The mechanism is half-shipped already: internal/shellintegration/scripts/nocx.bash computes
`compgen -c` in the background and sends it as an OSC 636 snapshot. This is the same thing
made request/response.

## Cost, stated

One extra shell per environment (trivial locally; over SSH another channel on the connection
already open), a script per shell family (bash and zsh differ), and cwd synchronisation —
OSC 7 already gives us that. The helper's environment is NOT the user's: exported variables
and functions defined interactively will not be there, and the candidates must say so rather
than pretend.

## Acceptance Criteria

On an SSH session, typing a partial path and pressing Tab completes it from the REMOTE
filesystem, and `git ch` + Tab offers checkout and cherry-pick from git's own completion —
both with the candidate's source naming the adapter, not a local guess. The cd/pushd/rmdir
table is deleted in the same change, because the shell now answers.

title: Flaky under load: TestBashSnapshotArrivesBeforeFirstPrompt fails when the machine is busy
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

Run `go test -race ./...` while the machine is loaded (two agent worktrees compiling plus a
dev stand was enough on 2026-08-02):

    --- FAIL: TestBashSnapshotArrivesBeforeFirstPrompt (0.63s)
        scripts_exec_test.go:862: the snapshot arrived AFTER the first prompt was usable:
        S at 280, first B at 147

Re-run on an idle machine, or with -count=3 in the same worktree, and it passes.

## Why it matters

The test asserts a real product property — the OSC 636 command-existence snapshot must be
there before the first prompt is usable, or highlighting and (now) completion have nothing
to answer from on the first command. But it asserts it by racing a 250 ms schedule against
`compgen -c`, so under load it reports a defect that is not there.

The cost is not the red line, it is what a red line teaches: this one was investigated as
"did the search change break the shell integration?" and needed a baseline run on the branch
to clear. A test that fails for reasons unrelated to the change is a test that trains people
to ignore it.

The script already degrades deliberately (on timeout the snapshot is left for a later
prompt), so the honest assertion is probably about the DEGRADE being correct rather than
about the race being won on a loaded machine — or the schedule needs to be injectable so the
test does not have to race a real clock.

## Acceptance Criteria

The test either does not depend on wall-clock scheduling, or it asserts the degrade path
explicitly; running the suite under load no longer produces this failure. Proven by running
it with the machine deliberately loaded.

title: Where advice lives: attached to its subject, and the conversation panel is a projection
description:
Owner's question, 2026-08-02: advice is not limited to the alternate screen — so does the AI
need its own panel?

The decision is not "panel or no panel" but WHERE ADVICE LIVES. In the ledger it is always
the same thing: an entry of kind=agent with a `cites` edge to its subject. The surfaces
follow from that, and none of them is "the AI panel":

- Advice about a block renders UNDER that block and scrolls with it. Reopen the session six
  months later and the failure and its explanation are adjacent, instead of being in a
  separate chat history you have to correlate by timestamp. This is the owner's original
  framing — AI inside the current block.
- Advice about the screen renders in a side rail or overlay, and only while the program is
  up. Here a panel IS required, for a physical reason rather than a taste one: the alternate
  screen owns the whole viewport and there is nowhere to put an inline row. The rail dies
  with the TUI; the entry stays in the ledger and later reads as an ordinary entry in the
  flow (nocx-x8s2).
- A long task spanning tabs gets a task/span view, because it has no single block to attach
  to — it IS the span.

The load-bearing rule: A CONVERSATION PANEL IS A PROJECTION, NOT A HOME (ADR-0019 rule 4) —
a filter over kind='agent' + conversation_id, disposable and rebuildable. A sidebar like
Warp's is fine. What is not fine is the conversation LIVING there: that recreates the second
timeline ADR-0019 rejected, where agent commands are visible in one place and human commands
in another and neither answers "what happened here".

Input stays one input (ADR-0004: the DOM editor owns the line), with an EXPLICIT switch. No
autodetection as the primary mechanism: it fails in both directions — a question lands in
bash, or a command lands in the model. Autodetection may later exist as a suggestion the
user confirms, never as a silent decision.

## Acceptance Criteria

An agent entry rendered under its block, an agent entry rendered in the alt-screen rail, and
the same entry listed in a conversation panel are all reading ONE row — proven by deleting
the panel's backing state and rebuilding it from the ledger with no loss.

title: The assistant on the alternate screen: explain, guide, and only then drive a TUI
description:
Owner's idea, 2026-08-02: while a full-screen program owns the terminal, the AI explains
what is on the screen, what the options are, what to choose — and eventually presses the
keys itself.

Why this is ours to build. AD-6 puts terminal render state in the frontend, so the
alternate screen is already a grid of cells with attributes, reachable by the same
mechanism that serializes a block's output (design §7). Claude Code cannot do this at all —
it never shares the user's terminal. Warp keeps agent work in a separate conversation
timeline. And ADR-0020's `awaiting-takeover` is already the exact state where a TUI owns
the lane: the ADR was amended so the agent is DEMOTED there (read + advise) rather than
evicted.

## The ladder — build in this order, each rung shippable alone

1. EXPLAIN (read-only). "What is this screen?" A screen snapshot goes to the model on
   explicit ask. Zero new authority, no staleness problem, and most of the value.
2. GUIDE (still read-only for us). "To do X, press Y." The human presses. Still no
   keystroke authority.
3. DRIVE. The agent sends the keys, under the staleness rule below and rule 6 of ADR-0020.

## The hard problem, and the proposed answer

STALENESS. A keystroke's meaning is entirely a function of the frame it lands in: the agent
reads frame N, the user or the program moves, and `y` answers a prompt nobody meant to
answer. So a proposed keystroke is bound to the SCREEN REVISION it was computed from, and
the lane REFUSES to deliver it if the screen has changed — optimistic concurrency, with the
screen generation as the token. This is not a nicety: it is the difference between an
assistant and a random-input generator.

Two consequences that follow:

- Effect classification cannot be derived from a keystroke. `y` means "yes" to whatever is
  showing; `x` kills a process in htop and deletes a character in vim. Under ADR-0020's
  policy this is permanently LOW confidence, so agent-driven input escalates by default and
  is only allowed to relax for programs we have a profile for.
- The agent must always know how to LEAVE. A program it cannot exit is a wedged lane, so a
  profile's known-safe quit sequence is a requirement of the profile, not an extra.

## What a program profile holds

Detection signature (alt-screen entry + first-frame shape), how to read state, keys known to
be destructive, and the safe quit sequence. Candidates: less, vim, htop/top, fzf,
`git rebase -i`, ncdu, k9s, lazygit, tmux.

## Screen capture is a data class, not a string

Plain text loses what matters: reverse video marks the selected row, colour carries state,
box drawing carries layout, and the cursor position is often the whole answer. The snapshot
is a structured artifact (grid + attributes + cursor + mouse-reporting mode), with the
capture provenance ADR-0019 §6 already requires. It is also FAR more sensitive than a
command line — a password prompt, a token in a pager — so it inherits the taint rules of
nocx-qopb and is never sent anywhere except on an explicit ask.

## Deliberately out for now

Mouse control ("click somewhere") needs the program's mouse-reporting mode, which the
frontend does know (SGR 1006) — but it lands after keystrokes work. Continuous
frame-by-frame driving is out: snapshot on demand or on quiescence (the inactivity signal
the lease already computes), never a per-frame loop, which is unaffordable in both latency
and tokens.

## Success Criteria

A user runs a full-screen program, asks what is on the screen, and gets an answer that names
the actual options visible — with no keystroke sent. Then, at the drive rung: a keystroke
proposed against a screen that has since changed is REFUSED by the lane rather than
delivered, proven by a test that mutates the screen between proposal and delivery.
acceptance_criteria: A user runs a full-screen program, asks what is on the screen, and gets an answer naming the options actually visible, with no keystroke sent. At the drive rung, a keystroke proposed against a screen that has since changed is refused by the lane rather than delivered.

title: Unlock by Touch ID instead of typing the passphrase (macOS)
description: Not a fix for anything broken — it makes the model we already have pleasant, which is a different priority and why it sits after the correctness beads. The point: what makes per-access unlock feel unreliable is that unlocking is expensive, so making it nearly free retires the 'ask at startup or on access' question rather than answering it. Security.framework with kSecAccessControlBiometryCurrentSet; note our keyring today is zalando/go-keyring, which shells out to /usr/bin/security and has no biometry path.
acceptance_criteria: On macOS the vault can be unsealed with Touch ID, with the passphrase remaining as the fallback; the content key is NOT gated by it and still opens unprompted at startup; the darwin-only cgo this needs does not reach the Linux or Windows builds and does not disturb the no-cgo SQLite decision (ADR-0018).

title: AGENTS.md is a contract, so it has to be readable in one sitting

acceptance_criteria: AGENTS.md keeps every rule and every enforced mechanic, with each rule's evidence compressed to one quotable line; the file is under ~400 lines excluding the managed Beads block; the anchors CLAUDE.md and docs/vision.md link to still resolve.

title: The pre-commit prettier gate only covers frontend/, despite claiming it covers the rest
description:
The pre-commit hook runs prettier as `cd frontend && npm run format:check`
(.githooks/pre-commit:122), so the check is rooted at frontend/ and sees only
frontend/**. Its own comment claims the opposite — "always: it covers markdown
and config the scoping misses" — which is why nobody noticed.

Everything outside frontend/ is therefore unformatted and unchecked: AGENTS.md,
README.md, docs/**, .github/workflows/**, Makefile, and contracts/**.

Found while landing nocx-ti8w: `npx prettier --check .` from the repo root
reports contracts/vault.resetPreview.schema.json as unformatted. It has been
that way since e7ea5b8 and no commit was ever blocked by it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `cd frontend && npm run format:check` — passes.
2. `npx prettier --check .` from the repo root — reports
   contracts/vault.resetPreview.schema.json.

## Acceptance Criteria

The pre-commit prettier gate covers the whole repository, not just frontend/,
and the existing violation is fixed so the gate is green from the first run. The
hook's comment matches what the command actually checks.

title: SSH session reconnects when the connection is lost, with an ask/auto/never setting
description:
No bead covers this today. nocx-2ho.3 is closed and is the AD-9 byte-offset replay layer (WebSocket drop, backend session survives); nocx-bwzg is a bug about two reconnect subscribers on a live session. Neither is 'the SSH connection died, get it back'.

Surfaced by the file-manager design (.internal/specs/2026-08-01-file-manager-design.md, nocx-gglz), which CONSUMES this: a dropped session leaves the Files panel and its viewer tabs readable but unrefreshable, and they rebind on reconnect only when the attested endpoint matches. The file manager works without this bead — just with no way back — so this is a dependency in the product sense, not a blocking edge.
acceptance_criteria: When an SSH session's connection is lost (not a WebSocket drop — AD-9 already covers that), nocx surfaces it and offers to reconnect; a setting chooses ask / auto / never; a reconnect that succeeds reports the endpoint it actually reached (resolved host, port, principal, jump route) so consumers can tell whether it is the same filesystem. Tested with: connection lost mid-session, reconnect to the same endpoint, reconnect after the profile was edited to a different host.

title: Verify the focus-drift keystroke lands exactly once, in a real browser
description: Split out of EDITOR-W4 (nocx-87o) on 2026-08-01 after a worker diagnosed the code rather than assuming a defect. terminal-content.ts _globalKeydown has two redirect paths that LOOK inconsistent and are not. Block-selected: preventDefault + focus + insertText, exactly one char, deterministic, asserted in jsdom. Focus-drifted (body has focus): focus() only, NO preventDefault — the event target is fixed at dispatch so CM6 never sees the keydown, but the browser's native default action runs afterwards against the then-focused contentDOM and lands the character once via beforeinput. jsdom CANNOT observe this: it performs no native text insertion, so a zero there is a harness artifact and asserting it would encode a falsehood. Hence a real browser. IMPORTANT for whoever takes this: the naive 'make both paths call insertText' fix DOUBLES the drift character (native default plus programmatic insert). The binding spec's framing would have produced exactly that regression.
acceptance_criteria: In Playwright against the real build: with focus on body and the editor visible, one printable keystroke puts exactly ONE character in the editor document. Same for the block-selected path. Both assertions present — the second is what keeps the first from being 'fixed' into a doubling.

title: Remove graphify from the repo — index, skill, hooks and docs
description: Owner decision 2026-08-01. Measured over one design-and-review session: five graphify queries, zero answers — it returns symbol names ranked by graph proximity, truncated to a token budget, while every finding that mattered came from grep (blocks.ts:671's serializeRange call, which made an entire byte-stream output-capture mechanism unnecessary; the absent z-index:20 that three comments still claim exists). Cost: 91MB of generated output committed across 16 commits, a PreToolUse hook making a graph query mandatory before EVERY file read and grep, and workers regenerating it unasked — one dropped 326k lines into a diff under review, which is how the question got asked. Removed: graphify-out/, .claude/skills/graphify/, .claude/CLAUDE.md, both settings.json hooks, and references in CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, README.md, .gitignore. AGENTS.md keeps a Code search section recording the measurement so nobody reintroduces an index or a pre-read hook without beating the grep baseline.
acceptance_criteria: No graphify files tracked; no hook fires before a file read; the only remaining mention is the AGENTS.md record of the removal.
close_reason: Removed in 6ca29c4: graphify-out/ (48 tracked files, 91MB), .claude/skills/graphify/, .claude/CLAUDE.md, both PreToolUse hooks, and the references in CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, README.md and .gitignore. AGENTS.md gains a Code search section recording the measurement so the decision is not re-argued from scratch.

Measured over one design-and-review session: five graphify queries, zero answers — it returns symbol names ranked by graph proximity, truncated to a token budget, while every finding that mattered came from grep (blocks.ts:671's serializeRange call, which made an entire output-capture mechanism unnecessary; the absent z-index:20 that three comments still claim). title: Reindex is an operation the size of years, and must not resurrect what was excluded
description: Design §5.2, §9.1. FTS corruption, a tokenizer upgrade, a schema migration or a change to the redaction rules all force a reindex of gigabytes of text. That needs: a schema version for the FTS projection separate from the main schema; a resumable rebuild with progress and cancel; a disk-space precondition; and search coverage that states the rebuild is in progress rather than answering as if complete. The trap worth naming, because it is silent: a reindex that re-derives from stored text can RESURRECT output previously excluded as sensitive. Exclusion must be recorded durably, not re-decided by re-running the matcher.
acceptance_criteria: Interrupt a rebuild at 40% and restart it: it resumes rather than restarting, and search says it is incomplete throughout. An artifact excluded from the index by a §9.1 decision is still excluded after a full reindex, without re-running the matcher.

title: An explicit target chip — never a magic prefix
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §8.2, §8.3. ADR-0004 rejects magic prefixes in those words: 'an explicit command/agent switch plus a keyboard shortcut, never a magic prefix such as ? — prefixes collide with valid shell syntax'. It is right on the merits: > is redirection, / begins an absolute path, @ is valid in arguments. A visible target chip with a shortcut to cycle it, and the current target rendered at all times so Enter is never a surprise. And when the shell target is unavailable, Enter does NOT silently become an agent question — a surface that reinterprets a keystroke by rank has broken the contract that makes a terminal usable.
acceptance_criteria: The active target is visible before Enter. No prefix character changes the submission target. With the shell target unavailable, Enter does not submit to another target without explicit activation.

title: The editor surface is reachable when the shell cannot vouch for it
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §8.1. Today shouldShowEditor(m.owned) ties the editor's existence to shell input ownership, so sshing to a box without our hooks removes the application's whole input surface. Three-way split: inline as today when the shell target is owned; reachable by a deliberate shortcut as an overlay in every other state; NEVER inline in alt-screen, where a persistent editor competes with vim and a debugger for keys and screen space. input-state.ts keeps its states, transitions and fail-open semantics untouched — what changes is who consumes owned. ADR-0004 §1 survives word for word.
acceptance_criteria: With no shell integration, the overlay is reachable by shortcut and no inline editor appears. In alt-screen the full viewport and raw keyboard behaviour are unchanged. PROMPT_READY behaviour is byte-identical to today.

title: Outcome annotation while typing
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §10.3. 'This failed here twice; the variant that worked was ... REGION=eu', shown as you compose, scoped to the environment and saying which rung it means. This is the recall data rendered at composition time rather than only inside the ranker — showing it is cheaper than being subtle about it in the ordering.
acceptance_criteria: Composing a command that failed in this environment shows the count and the successor. The annotation names its scope. A command with no history shows nothing — the annotation is silent by default.

title: Passive context, always; confirmation only when the situation is unusual
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §10.2. The affected facets appear next to the pending command — no modal, no keystroke, no interruption. Confirmation escalates only on criticality != routine, privilege elevated relative to the session norm, or a key facet at confidence=unknown.
acceptance_criteria: Local rm -rf node_modules in a routine environment: context shown, nothing blocked. The same command on an environment marked critical: confirmation required. Turning the passive display off is a setting; the escalation is not.

title: The terminal warns you where you are, before Enter
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §10.2, §10.3.

Most of a terminal's memory is spent showing you what already happened; the leverage is in what it can tell you while you can still change your mind.

The rule that keeps this from becoming wallpaper is the whole design: SHOW ALWAYS, CONFIRM RARELY. A guardrail that fires on the verb alone gets trained away within a week and then fails to fire on the one that mattered — which is exactly the failure mode of a generic 'are you sure?'. The escalation condition is not about the command, it is about where you are, and that is a sentence only a design with Environment can write.
acceptance_criteria: A destructive command in a routine environment with no elevated privilege shows the context and asks nothing. The same command with criticality=critical, or elevated privilege, or a key facet at confidence=unknown, requires confirmation. Both halves are tested — the first is what keeps the second effective.

title: A destructive-shape classifier over the composed text
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §10.2. Recognise commands that destroy something — rm -rf, drop table, kubectl delete, terraform apply, redirection over a device. Runs on the composed text in the editor, where CM6 shell mode already parses it. It classifies shape only; it never decides whether to interrupt (that is the escalation rule).
acceptance_criteria: Known destructive shapes are recognised, including through a leading sudo and inside a simple pipeline. A false positive is a logged, tunable rule, not a code change.

title: History that remembers outcomes, not just text
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §10.4, §3.4. If make deploy failed twice here and 'make deploy REGION=eu' is its successor that worked, recall offers the successor and annotates the failure. Frequency alone systematically promotes mistakes, because a command you got wrong three times is frequent. Needs the rerun-of/supersedes edges written when a user edits and re-runs, plus the outcome feature in the scorer.
acceptance_criteria: Given a failed command and its edited successor that succeeded, recall ranks the successor first and the failure carries its annotation. A command with no successor ranks unchanged.

title: Doubtful text is retained but not indexed, and 'forget this output' is the escape hatch
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §9.1. When a matcher fires with low confidence the entry keeps its output and stays out of FTS — search that cannot find something is a smaller failure than search that surfaces a token by substring. And because rule-based redaction is allowed to be imperfect, a one-action 'forget this output' must exist: it drops the artifact and its index row in one transaction, and the entry survives.
acceptance_criteria: A low-confidence match retains the artifact and produces no FTS row. 'Forget this output' leaves the entry, removes the artifact, and leaves no index row behind — verified after a forced crash mid-operation.

title: do-not-record: a scope, not a vague promise
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §9. Per-session, toggled from the surface, does not survive a restart, suppresses ledger.open and artifact capture together. A global default lives in settings as public config. The earlier design mentioned the mode three times and never said what it covered.
acceptance_criteria: With the mode on, no entry row and no artifact is created for that session. Restarting the app clears it. The global default is a setting, not a hardcoded constant.

title: command-ledger.ts becomes the live cache, not a second writer
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §4.2, §6.2. The in-memory ledger stays as the frontend's render cache and ShellDriver's backing store. It must not grow its own path to the database, and it must never answer a recall query with its own ordering — ledger.query is the only ordering implementation, or the same keystroke returns different results depending on which tab it came from.
acceptance_criteria: grep shows exactly one caller path from the frontend to ledger.*. A recall query issued from two different tabs returns identically ordered results.

title: The file picker is native where the platform has one
description:
## Success Criteria

Wails v2.13 exposes runtime.OpenFileDialog(ctx, opts) (string, error) and runtime.OnFileDrop(ctx, cb) — both Go-side only, both returning absolute paths. The renderer reaches them through a new control-plane method rather than directly, per AD-1.

Path mode gets a chooser that yields a real absolute path. Where the runtime is absent — the dev-web harness has no Wails at all — the method reports itself unavailable and the surface falls back to what it does today: typing the path by hand, and reading contents in choose-file mode.

Drag-and-drop of a key file onto the connection editor is in scope if OnFileDrop is wired; say so if it is deferred.
acceptance_criteria: A control-plane method opens the native dialog and returns an absolute path; Path mode offers a chooser that uses it; the absence of the runtime is reported as unavailable rather than failing, and the surface degrades to manual entry; the method has a schema in contracts/.
close_reason: Landed in 758eed5

title: The Secrets page has no gutter and does not look like Connections
description:
## Steps to Reproduce
1. Settings → Secrets with the vault unlocked and secrets present.

## Expected
The page reads like Connections: a pinned toolbar with a filter and the create action, rows below, and the same gutter.

## Actual
Content sits flush against the rail and rows run past the right edge. The page is declared scrollMode 'contained' — the mode for surfaces that own their own scrolling, like Connections — but unlike Connections it is not built on CollectionView, so it gets neither the page gutter nor a toolbar. The store name was also bare text running into the row's edge.
acceptance_criteria: Secrets is a CollectionView with a filter and the add action in the toolbar; the add action is present on an empty vault; a filter that matches nothing says so rather than claiming the vault is empty; the store is a Badge.
close_reason: Landed

title: Rotating a secret overwrites the name the user gave it
description:
## Steps to Reproduce
1. Rename a secret on the Secrets page.
2. Rotate it (save a new password on the connection that owns it).

## Expected
The user's name survives, or the user is told it will not.

## Actual
Rotation writes a freshly generated user@host name over the one the user chose. Reported by the worker implementing ADR-0016.
acceptance_criteria: A generated name never replaces a user-supplied one; decide and record whether rotation carries the old name forward or asks.

title: vault.resetPreview undercounts secrets nothing references
description:
## Steps to Reproduce
1. Create a secret on the Secrets page with no connection using it.
2. Settings → Vault → Reset the vault.

## Expected
The confirmation counts it among what will be destroyed.

## Actual
It is not counted. vaultreset builds its preview from CountSecretReferences, which walks credential records — and an ownerless secret has no reference to walk. Reported by the worker implementing ADR-0016, whose change is what made ownerless secrets possible.
acceptance_criteria: The reset preview counts records the vault holds, not only references the credentials carry; a secret with no owner appears in the confirmation.

title: A secret owns its name (ADR-0016)
description:
## Success Criteria

See docs/decisions/0016-a-secret-owns-its-name.md. The ADR reverses the secrets-and-vault design spec §4.1; this epic is the work it implies.

Deliberately out of scope: changing the SecretID grammar, accepting a name as an identifier from the renderer, and storing secret values anywhere but a provider.
acceptance_criteria: The vault persists a display name per SecretID and is its only owner; a password saved on a connection gets a generated name; the Secrets page can add a secret with no connection using it, and rename one; a secret whose name did not land still renders, never blank and never as its id; '+ New Credential' is gone from the connection editor while selecting an existing credential remains; the design spec's 'No display name' clause is amended to point at ADR-0016.

title: The dialog sizes to the section it is showing, and the change is animated
description:
## Success Criteria

Tabs stops sizing its panel box to the tallest section and sizes it to the active one, so the New Group dialog's General section no longer sits in a box measured for Connection-with-Paste-key and the footer no longer floats hundreds of pixels below the last field. The panel height animates between sizes so the footer moves visibly rather than teleporting, and the animation is disabled under prefers-reduced-motion.

This reverses the sizing half of the Tabs decision recorded in ui/README.md ("every section is rendered into one grid cell, so the box is the size of the largest"). That decision traded emptiness for stability; the animation buys the stability back without the emptiness, so the README section must be rewritten rather than merely contradicted.

## Constraint that decides the technique

Transitioning to and from height:auto needs interpolate-size/calc-size, which is above both declared browser floors (WebKitGTK 2.40, Safari 16.2 — ADR-0013 §3). So the animation is measure-and-transition in JS: read the current height, pin it, set the target, transition, release to auto on transitionend. Dialog already owns the panel and its max-height, so it is the right place for it — not the surface.
acceptance_criteria: Switching sections or auth methods leaves no empty space below the footer; the panel height transitions rather than jumping; prefers-reduced-motion disables the transition; the panel never exceeds its viewport max-height mid-animation; ui/README.md's Tabs sizing section states the new trade.
close_reason: Landed in 3c952d2

title: A dialog names its width but not its height, so revealing a field moves the footer
description:
## Steps to Reproduce
1. Connections → New connection → Authentication.
2. Choose Public Key.

## Expected
The dialog does not change size.

## Actual
It grows: Public Key reveals a Path/Choose file/Paste key control and a field under it, and the footer buttons move down from under the pointer reaching for them. Tabs measures its sections so switching General/Authentication/Advanced is stable, but a control changing what its own section renders is outside that guarantee. The panel names its width via data-size and left its height to the content.
acceptance_criteria: The lg panel names a min-height bounded by its existing viewport max-height; choosing any auth method leaves the panel the same size.
close_reason: Landed

title: Copying a one-time recovery code reports nothing, including when it fails
description:
## Steps to Reproduce
1. Set up vault protection.
2. On the recovery-code step, press Copy.

## Expected
The user knows whether the code reached the clipboard.

## Actual
Nothing is shown. Both copy handlers swallow the rejection — one with a bare catch, one with an empty rejection arm — so a denied or unavailable clipboard is indistinguishable from a successful copy. The code is shown exactly once, so the user presses Done believing it is saved and it is gone for good.
acceptance_criteria: Both copy handlers report success and failure; the failure message says to write the code down before closing; tests cover both outcomes.
close_reason: Landed

title: Diagnostics rows touch, and Secrets floats a description line above every state
description:
## Steps to Reproduce
1. Settings → Vault → expand Diagnostics.
2. Settings → Secrets with the vault locked.

## Expected
Diagnostics rows are spaced like every other row group on the page. The locked Secrets page shows a locked state and one action.

## Actual
The diagnostics rows are a bare div, so nothing spaces them and they sit flush against each other. The Secrets page draws a standing line of body copy above every state, so a locked vault shows a paragraph with no heading over it and a centred plate floating below — contradicting the surface spec's own rule for the sealed state.
acceptance_criteria: Diagnostics rows are spaced by the Stack primitive; the Secrets explanation is the Secrets section's description and does not appear in the locked or empty states.
close_reason: Landed in b25db08

title: Every JSON-RPC method the renderer calls has a contract in contracts/
description:
## Success Criteria

Filled in as methods are touched, not in one sweep — the rule in AGENTS.md is that a method you add or change gets its contract in the same commit. This epic exists so the remaining surface is visible and can be swept once the touch-driven pass stops finding new ones.

vault.status landed with nocx-nfld.5, together with the Go and TypeScript harnesses both sides reuse.
acceptance_criteria: Every vault.*, profiles.*, settings.* and connection.* method the renderer calls has a fully-populated sample in contracts/, a Go shape test and a TypeScript key-list test; a method added or changed without one fails review. Deliberately out of scope: the binary data plane, which has no JSON shape to pin.

title: Diagnostics states values as badges at readable size, not fine print
acceptance_criteria: Badge gains a success tone; every diagnostics value is a Badge; the block is not set in a smaller type size than the page.

acceptance_criteria: Pressing Test raises a toast naming the store and its result; the timestamp stays as the record of when.

title: The Secrets page anchors its locked and empty states instead of floating them
acceptance_criteria: EmptyState takes an optional icon and fills the height it is given; the Secrets rows are built from kit components rather than .sr-row markup with emoji.

title: The backend's log is written into a mktemp dir nothing surfaces
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. `make dev-web > somewhere.log 2>&1`
2. Exercise anything that logs on the backend — unseal the vault, save a secret.
3. Read somewhere.log. It contains vite's output and not one line from the Go process.

## Why

scripts/dev-web.sh:115 runs the backend as `"$work/devharness" >"$work/backend.log" 2>&1`
where `$work` is a `mktemp -d`. Nothing prints that path, so capturing the script's own
output captures vite and nothing else.

## Cost

Several hours of one night. Diagnosing nocx-25k9.20 proceeded entirely by elimination —
ruling out a race, a stale frontend status, the idle timer, a second vault instance — while
the answer sat in that file the whole time, one WARN line:

    msg="provider put failed" provider=file error="vault is sealed"

which names the culprit immediately.
acceptance_criteria: make dev-web prints where the backend log is, or tees it to a stable path. A developer can read the backend's own INFO and WARN output without first reading scripts/dev-web.sh.

title: Every vault.status call writes to the OS keychain, though the spec says probe once
description:
Found while verifying a worker's caveat about the new "Test" button on the Vault page. The
worker reported that it could only wire Test to a status refresh because no re-probe RPC
exists, and worried the button therefore does nothing. The opposite is true, and that is the
defect.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Settings -> Vault. The page fetches vault.status on mount and after every operation.
2. Each fetch reaches system.Provider.Status(), which delegates straight to Probe()
   (internal/vault/system/system.go:122-124).
3. Probe() writes a random entry into the OS keychain, reads it back, compares the bytes and
   deletes it (:128 onward) — a real write per call, every call.

## Why it matters

- The spec is explicit and the code does not follow it. Vault design 5.7: the probe's
  "outcome is cached for the process lifetime with an explicit re-probe action". There is no
  cache and no re-probe action; there is only an unconditional probe on every status read.
- On macOS a keychain write can raise an OS authorisation prompt. A settings page that
  probes on mount can therefore prompt the user for merely opening it.
- A failed delete leaves an artifact. The spec accepts that as the price of a truthful probe
  ("preferable to a false positive") — but it accepted it for an occasional probe, not for
  one per page render.

## The two halves are linked, so fix them together

Adding the cache without an explicit re-probe RPC breaks the Test button, which is honest
today precisely BECAUSE nothing is cached. So: cache the outcome for the process lifetime,
add the re-probe method the spec already assumes, and point Test at it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Two vault.status calls in a row perform exactly one probe — asserted with a fake keyring
  that counts Set calls.
- An explicit re-probe path exists, is what the Vault page's Test button calls, and a test
  asserts it does perform a fresh probe.
- The cached outcome is invalidated when the process would otherwise report stale readiness
  after a store's state changed — state which case you chose and why, in the code.

title: The Tabs status marker distinguishes states by colour alone
description:
Found reviewing the worker diff for nocx-0v7z before merging it. The mechanism is right and
the screen-reader half is correct; the sighted-but-colour-blind half is missing.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Render a vertical Tabs with three items whose statuses are ok, warning and error.
2. View it with a red-green colour vision deficiency (or desaturate the screenshot).
3. The three rows are indistinguishable.

## Why it happens

`styles/components/tabs.css` gives `.ui-tabs__status` an 8px circle whose ONLY difference
between tones is `background`: `--color-success` / `--color-warning` / `--color-danger`. The
accessible name is handled properly — a `.ui-visually-hidden` span inside the row's Button —
so assistive technology is fine. A sighted user who cannot separate those hues has nothing
else to go on.

That matters here more than it usually would. The marker exists so the broken store can be
spotted WITHOUT selecting its row (the Vault page's store rail, spec §7). Selecting the row
shows the state in words — which is exactly the step the marker is supposed to save.

WCAG 1.4.1: colour must not be the only visual means of conveying information.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The three tones differ by something other than hue — a glyph, a shape, or a fill pattern —
  and a test asserts the distinguishing attribute reaches the DOM per tone.
- The `.ui-visually-hidden` accessible name stays as it is; this bead does not change it.
- The kit README's Tabs row records how tones are distinguished, so the next variance does
  not reintroduce colour-only.

title: Quick connect sits 80px narrower than its own dialog
description:
Reported from the running app: the quick-connect palette's filter field and rows
stop well short of the dialog's right edge, leaving a band of dead space beside
them.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the quick-connect palette (the connection picker).
2. The panel's border is at one width; the search field and every row end ~80px
   before it.

## Why it happens

Two owners for one dimension, which is the exact thing dialog.css:32-38 forbids in
words: "The size prop names the width; the content never gets a say."

- dialog.css:86 — `.nocx-dialog__panel[data-size='lg'] { width: 640px }`
- quick-connect.css — `.quick-connect { width: 512px }`

640 minus 24px of panel padding on each side is a 592px content box; the palette
declared 512. The stale comment above the dialog rule preserves the history: it
still describes the content as "512px + the 24px padding on each side", i.e. a
560px panel. Someone widened the panel to 640 and neither the content width nor
the comment followed.

## Fix

quick-connect.css stops naming a width (`width: 100%`), and the comment on the
dialog rule now says the number is declared there and only there. The fixed
HEIGHT stays: it is what keeps rows from moving under the pointer while filtering,
and that argument is about the list, not the panel.

## Acceptance Criteria

- No stylesheet outside dialog.css declares a width for a Dialog's content at
  any size.
- The quick-connect filter field and its rows span the dialog's full content box.
- Verified in the running app, not only by reading the rule.

title: The settings-page gate names Vault instead of walking the page registry
description:
Follow-up from nocx-d3mr, recorded because I accepted a weaker gate than the brief asked for rather than closing over it.

The brief required a test that walks the registered settings pages, so that a NEW page opting out fails it. What landed in 7272280 (frontend/src/settings.test.ts) is two tests: one mounts the generated pages, one mounts VaultSection by name. A page added tomorrow is not covered by either.

Why this is P2 and not P1: after nocx-d3mr the protection lives in the DEFAULT — a horizontal Field is primary unless a caller explicitly passes labelProminence='secondary', and no surface passes it. So the gate guards against a deliberate opt-out, not against forgetting, and forgetting was the original failure mode.

Cost to do it properly: the component pages need clients (ProfileClient, VaultClient, VaultController), so the test needs the same mock scaffolding settings.test.ts already builds for VaultSection, applied over the registry instead of one name.
acceptance_criteria: A test enumerates the registered settings pages (settingsPages() in settings.tsx) and mounts each one's renderContent(), asserting every rendered .ui-field-horizontal carries data-label='primary'. Adding a page that opts out fails the test without anyone editing it.

title: Transition to writing-plans
close_reason: Brainstorming session complete

title: You cannot see what the vault holds
description:
Asked by the user looking at the Vault page: "how do I even see what is in my
vault?" There is no answer in the product today.

The transport exposes nine vault methods (internal/transport/ws_vault.go:112-128):
status, setup, unseal, seal, changePassphrase, regenerateRecovery,
setDefaultProvider, setAutoSeal, activity. None of them enumerates what is stored.

The closest thing that exists is `credentials.list` + `credentials.hasPassword`
(frontend/src/profiles.ts:397,417), on a different page, answering a different
question: which credential records exist, and whether each has a password. That is
a view of the credential list, not an inventory of the vault — it cannot show a
secret held for a profile that no longer exists, which is exactly what nocx-2x8x
(orphan collection) is about.

## What this is not

Not a request to reveal secrets. Reading a secret back in plaintext was ruled out
deliberately (nocx-ggja verified "no Reveal or plaintext read-back path anywhere").
The inventory is metadata only: what is held, for what, in which provider, when it
was written.

## Open question for whoever picks this up

Whether this belongs on the Vault page or on Credentials is a product decision, not
an implementation detail. The Vault page currently shows plumbing — default
provider, per-provider Writable/Not ready badges — which is a maintainer's view of
the subsystem. An inventory is the first thing on that page that would answer a
user's question rather than an implementer's.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A user can see, without leaving the app, what the vault holds: one row per stored
  secret with what it belongs to, which provider holds it, and when it was written.
- Nothing in the path returns or renders a secret value.
- The list distinguishes a secret whose owner still exists from one whose owner does
  not, so an orphan is visible rather than inferred (see nocx-2x8x).
- A test walks the path a user walks: from an empty vault, save a secret, and assert
  the row appears with the right owner and provider.
notes:
CORRECTION to my own acceptance criteria, found in the KB check before any work started: the criterion 'the list distinguishes a secret whose owner still exists from one whose owner does not' is NOT achievable as written.

internal/vault/provider.go:16-28 — Provider is ID/Status/Get, WritableProvider adds Put/Delete. There is no List anywhere. And per the stored memory constraint-nocx-secrets-zalando-go-keyring-v0-2, zalando/go-keyring v0.2.8 exposes exactly Set, Get, Delete and DeleteAll — the system provider CANNOT enumerate what it holds, at any level.

Spec 4.1 is the reason it is not merely missing: a vault catalogue document mapping SecretID to provider/name/kind/timestamps was proposed in the first draft and killed in peer review on three counts (two persisted owners for name and kind, the all-or-nothing metadata guarantee from nocx-y910.1, a third crash gap per write). SecretID is deliberately 'not promoted into a durable user-facing entry identity'.

So an inventory must be DERIVED from metadata that already exists (credentials.list + hasPassword, profiles holding references), not read from the providers. That view can show everything a user owns; it cannot show an orphan, because an orphan is by definition the thing metadata no longer names. Orphans stay nocx-dm0's problem and would need a List capability on the file provider plus an accepted blind spot on system.

title: The file provider tells you to unlock a login keychain it never uses
description:
On the Vault page the `file` provider renders: "Your login keychain is locked.
Unlock it and try again." The file provider is nocx's own encrypted blob. It has
no login keychain, so the remedy named is not merely unhelpful — it is impossible
to act on, and it sends the user to an OS dialog that cannot change anything.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Settings → Vault with an uninitialized (or sealed) vault.
2. Providers section, row `file`: badges "Writable" + "Not ready", message
   "Your login keychain is locked. Unlock it and try again."

## Why it happens

internal/vault/file/file.go:62-69 — `Status` returns
`vault.Status{Ready: false, Reason: vault.ReasonLocked}` whenever `p.dataKey == nil`,
i.e. whenever the vault is sealed or not yet set up.

frontend/src/vault.tsx:35 — `REASON_MESSAGES.locked` is written for the OS keyring:
"Your login keychain is locked. Unlock it and try again."

So one reason code is carrying two unrelated meanings — "the OS keychain is locked"
and "this vault is sealed" — and the UI prints the first for both. The truthful
sentence for `file` is that the vault is sealed and unsealing it is the remedy,
which is a different action in a different place.

## Relationship to nocx-25k9.6

Same family, different instance, and they must not be merged: 25k9.6 is the SYSTEM
provider's probe classifying a locked collection as no-service. This one is the FILE
provider borrowing a keychain-specific message for an unrelated state. 25k9.6 is
being worked now; whoever takes this should expect to touch the same message map and
coordinate.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The `file` provider's not-ready state is distinguishable from an OS-keyring lock:
  either a reason of its own or a provider-aware message, decided deliberately.
- The rendered sentence for a not-ready `file` provider names an action the user can
  actually take on this machine, and a test pins the sentence to the state.
- No reason code carries two meanings: a test asserts each Reason maps to exactly
  one user-facing remedy, per provider.
notes:
Widened after an independent review (codex) and my own verification: this is a LAYERING defect, not a wording one, and it has three faces.

1. provider.go:9-10 states the contract in words: a Provider 'knows nothing about sealing, routing or policy'. The file provider knows about all three — file.go:192 has its own Lock(), Get/Put return ErrVaultSealed, and Status() reports the vault's seal as its own unavailability. The implementation contradicts the interface's own doc comment.

2. file.go:117-141 — when no blob exists yet, Unlock deliberately starts empty and the doc comment says the provider is 'ready to accept writes; the first mutation creates the blob lazily'. But dataKey stays nil, so Status() (file.go:62-69) reports Ready=false Reason=locked for exactly that state. The comment and the status disagree about the same moment.

3. provider.go:42 puts ReasonUnknownProvider in the same enum. That is not a status a registered provider can ever report — it is a reference-ROUTING failure. Registry state, external-service health and vault lifecycle are collapsed into one bag of strings.

Suggested shape rather than a patch: separate provider availability (available/unavailable/unknown + why) from vault lifecycle (uninitialized/sealed/unsealed) from reference-resolution errors (unknown-provider/secret-missing/corrupt-store). The spec justified the binary Ready on the grounds that CI cannot exercise a third value (design doc 269-274); that is a testability argument erasing a distinction that drives different user remedies, and it is what produced the impossible 'unlock your login keychain' advice.
close_reason:
Landed in f2c41f5. file.Provider.Status() probes the document store and answers about it; a sealed vault with a readable store is Ready. ReasonUnknownProvider left the provider Reason enum for vault.go as a routing error, wire value unchanged so the renderer mapping still resolves. go test -race ./internal/vault/... green including the invariant this could have broken — a sealed vault still refuses Get/Put/Delete, proven by test.

ACCEPTED WITH A KNOWN WART, recorded rather than closed over: any docs.Read error is reported as ReasonDenied, which overclaims — a corrupt document and an I/O failure are not access denials. There is no store-level reason in the current vocabulary to say it honestly, which is precisely the wider split the design asks for (spec §5, and codex's four-way separation of provider availability / vault lifecycle / reference-resolution errors). Fix it there, not by adding one more string here.

Second wart: Status now reads and parses the whole blob under p.mu on every call, where it used to be an in-memory check. Harmless at today's call rate, wasteful at any scale.

Import runs through the Vault, so an uninitialized or sealed vault surfaces setup or unlock rather than a generic failure.
